docs.title: django-spec-html
docs.text:
A django-service-specs spec served over plain Django, with no API framework between the request and the kernel's dispatch. Two halves, and the admin face the pages are served from too:

  • Pages. SpecFormView serves a spec whose Validator is a Django form as the page a person fills that form in on. A refused post comes back as the page again, with the refusal placed on its form. An htmx request is answered with a fragment of the same page (an htmx request).
  • Serving a read. SpecSelectorView serves a selector spec as a list page, filtered and paged, or as one row's page, and the available and unavailable filters ask each row what its operations allow and why not.
  • JSON views. SpecView, AsyncSpecView and the functions they are built from serve a spec as JSON, for a script or a fetch().
  • In the admin. SpecActionsMixin serves a spec's page as a Django admin action, on one row from its change page or on the rows selected in its changelist, inside the admin's chrome and its scope.
from django_spec_html import SpecActionsMixin, SpecFormView, SpecSelectorView, SpecView

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-html

It installs django-service-specs, the kernel whose specs it serves, from 0.33.0, on Python 3.10 and Django 4.2 or later. The JSON views need no entry in INSTALLED_APPS; the pages' default templates are found as any app's are, so list django_spec_html there to use them, or give each page a template_name of its own (the page's template).

Both halves were the kernel's, and moved here so the kernel carries no transport: the JSON views as kernel 0.11.0 shipped them, and SpecFormView as kernel 0.5.1 did. The behaviour is the kernel's, but for the page answering an UnsupportedMediaType an operation raises at 415 where the kernel's answered 400 (refusals on the page); the import path is this package's. The kernel no longer ships these names: import them from django_spec_html.

docs.title: In the admin
docs.text:
A spec's page served as a Django admin action: the same declaration, the same page and the same checks, inside the admin's chrome. SpecActionsMixin is a ModelAdmin that offers each spec it declares as an action, and serves it with the page that serves it anywhere else, SpecFormView for a spec with a FormValidator and SpecConfirmView for one with none. The admin supplies the templates and the styling; nothing about the operation is restated for it.

from django_spec_html import SpecAction, SpecActionsMixin

This is not a framework for admin actions. django-object-actions and django-admin-confirm are maintained and better at being one. The admin face exists so that one declaration reaches the admin as well, with its own permission checks, its target and its confirmation intact.

docs.title: Two kinds of action
docs.text:
Which kind is the spec's target's answer, never the declaration's:

The spec's target The action Where it is offered an instance_selector_spec an object action, on one row a link among the change page's object tools a collection_selector_spec a changelist action, on the selected rows an entry in the changelist's action dropdown

A spec with neither, a create, and a many spec, whose page is SpecFormSetView's, are not admin actions: the mixin refuses them when the admin is registered.

The example declares one of each. Withdrawing a book acts on the row, and has nothing to fill in; repricing acts on the selected books, and asks for the price:

class IsEditor(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Only an editor may change the catalogue."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.has_perm("adapter_app.change_book")


@dataclasses.dataclass
class BookOut:
    pk: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    status: Status


def book_by_pk(*, pk: int) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.filter(pk=pk)


def withdraw(*, instance: Book) -> Book:
    instance.status = Status.DRAFT
    instance.save(update_fields=["status"])
    return instance


# One row: an object action, linked from the book's change page.
withdraw_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=withdraw,
    permissions=[IsEditor()],
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=book_by_pk,
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
)


class PriceForm(forms.Form):
    price = forms.DecimalField(max_digits=6, decimal_places=2, min_value=Decimal("0"))


def published(*, pks: list[int]) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    # Only the published rows, whatever was ticked.
    return Book.objects.filter(pk__in=pks, status=Status.PUBLISHED)


def reprice(*, collection: QuerySet[Book], data: dict[str, Any]) -> int:
    return collection.update(price=data["price"])


# A set: a changelist action, offered in the action dropdown.
reprice_books_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=reprice,
    permissions=[IsEditor()],
    validator=FormValidator(PriceForm),
    collection_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=published,
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pks", "array", items="integer", required=True)),
    ),
)

The selector behind the changelist action decides the set: it takes the ticked primary keys and keeps only the published books among them, so a row the selector does not return is never repriced, whatever was ticked.

Each is a SpecAction on the admin's spec_actions: a name, the spec, the label the admin shows, and the parameter of the target selector the admin fills. Register the admin as any other:

class BookAdmin(SpecActionsMixin, admin.ModelAdmin):
    spec_actions = (
        SpecAction(
            "withdraw",
            withdraw_book_spec,
            "Withdraw",
            # The change page's object id fills the selector's pk.
            parameter="pk",
            page_kwargs={"display_target": True, "success_message": "Book withdrawn."},
        ),
        SpecAction(
            "reprice",
            reprice_books_spec,
            "Reprice selected %(verbose_name_plural)s",
            # The selected rows' keys fill the selector's pks.
            parameter="pks",
            page_kwargs={"success_message": "Repriced at %(price)s."},
        ),
    )

docs.title: The URL each action is served at
docs.text:
get_urls() adds one URL per action, ahead of the admin's own and each wrapped in admin_site.admin_view(), so only a signed-in staff member the site admits reaches it, and anyone else is sent to the admin's sign-in page:

The action Its URL Its name object <object_id>/actions/<name>/ admin:<app>_<model>_<name> changelist actions/<name>/ admin:<app>_<model>_<name>

An object action fills its parameter with the change page's object_id, through the page's route_kwargs, unquoted as the admin quotes a key into its URLs.

A changelist action is an entry in the dropdown that redirects to its page with the selected rows' primary keys in the query string, repeated under its parameter (?pks=3&pks=5), which must be an array the collection selector reads. The page binds them to that parameter as server_arguments, read from the query string on GET and on the post the page sends back to its own URL. So nothing posted stands in for the selection: a value posted under the name is dropped, as every value a binding answers for is. The keys are first narrowed to the admin's get_queryset(), as the changelist narrows the rows its own actions run on, so a key outside it never reaches the selector (the admin's scope). Within that, the selector still decides the set: a key it does not answer is not acted on, so the example reprices the published books among those ticked and leaves a draft as it was. A key the parameter or the primary key refuses, ?pks=abc, is a 400.

The keys travel in the URL, so a selection is as long as a URL and as the parameter takes: an array past its max_length, or past the kernel's SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH where it declares none, is refused at 400. Selecting every row of a long changelist is a filter's job, declared on the selector, rather than a list of keys.

docs.title: The admin's scope comes first
docs.text:
A page is the admin's as much as its change page is, so it answers to the admin's own gates before the spec's, as Django's actions and change page do:

  • The admin's permission. A page is served only to a principal the ModelAdmin's has_view_or_change_permission() admits, asked of the row on an object action; anyone else is refused with a 403.
  • The admin's rows. An object action's row is the admin's get_object(), read from its get_queryset(), so a row outside it, which get_object() finds no row for, is a 404. The change page redirects such a key to the admin's index with a message instead; the action's page answers it as any route does a row not found. A changelist action's selection is narrowed to the same queryset before it is bound.

The spec's own checks run inside that scope, on every request, the object-level check included, and its selector decides the set within it. So an admin whose get_queryset() shows each staff member their own rows keeps every other row from its spec actions too, whatever the spec's checks or selector would admit, and neither the URL nor the query string reaches past it.

docs.title: Who is offered an action
docs.text:
Only a principal the spec and the admin both admit. The object-tools link and the dropdown entry are shown where the kernel's authorize, the spec's class-level check, admits the signed-in principal, asked with the page's own seeds and call context, stamped "html" as the page's call is (what a callable reads), and the admin's has_view_or_change_permission() does too. The admin's model permissions are not the whole gate: Django offers an action that declares no allowed_permissions to anyone who can view the changelist, and a spec's checks say what its operation needs whatever the admin shows. So the example's IsEditor decides as well, and a staff member who may view the books and is not an editor sees neither the link nor the entry.

The offer is advice. The page's own checks are the gate: a principal who reaches the URL directly is admitted or refused by the admin's scope and the spec, as on any route, and a refusal is the admin's 403. An entry not offered is not among get_actions(), which the changelist reads again on the post that runs an action, so posting its name runs nothing.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
The page is the spec's page, with every attribute it takes. page_kwargs hands it any keyword its as_view() takes - display_target, commit_button, asked_fields, success_message, pool_seeds - and as_view() checks them when the admin is registered, as it checks any page. The mixin answers for the rest, and refuses them in page_kwargs: the spec, the templates, success_url, route_kwargs, and server_arguments with get_server_arguments, since the binding is a changelist action's selection; a value the server answers for comes from a pool seed instead.

Its templates are django_spec_html/admin/spec_form.html and django_spec_html/admin/spec_confirm.html. Each extends admin/base_site.html - the admin's header, its stylesheets, the form's media, the action's label as the title and breadcrumbs back through the changelist and the row - around the very fragment the shipped page includes, so an htmx request is answered with that fragment, as it is anywhere else. The context is the page's, with the admin site's own each_context(), opts, title, spec_action, object_id on an object action and has_view_permission added. Override either template the Django way, in a directory of the project's own.

A success returns to the admin: an object action to the row's change page, a changelist action to the changelist, with the page's success_message among the admin's messages. A refusal is the admin page again with the refusal on its form, at the status any page answers it with, and a question a service asks with AdditionalInputRequired is asked there too.

The change page is rendered from django_spec_html/admin/change_form.html, which extends admin/change_form.html and lists the object actions ahead of the admin's own tools. A ModelAdmin with a change_form_template of its own extends that template to keep the links.

docs.title: The confirmation gates the form route only
docs.text: The page's confirmation, a question a service asks and a person answers, is the admin page's own, and gates the post a person sends from it. It is no gate on an agent route. The spec is one declaration for every route, and where the admin also offers an agent - a sidebar any page extending the admin's base carries, this one included - the same operation is reachable a second time, through the agent, on the same page. There the AdditionalInputRequired goes back to the model, which can answer it itself, as Confirming an operation says. The human gate on that route is the agent runtime's: django-spec-agents' ToolGuard, whose approval card a person answers before the tool runs.

docs.title: What is refused when the admin is registered
docs.text:
The pages are built when the ModelAdmin is, at admin.site.register or @admin.register, so a declaration the admin could not serve fails the project's start rather than its first request. ImproperlyConfigured names the admin and the action, for:

  • an entry that is not a SpecAction;
  • a name that is not a slug, is used twice, or is one of the admin's own URL names for the model (add, change, changelist, delete, history);
  • a label that does not format with the model's names, as Django formats an action's description for the dropdown and as the link and the page's title are formatted too: %(verbose_name)s and %(verbose_name_plural)s are the names, and a literal % is written %%;
  • a spec that is not a ServiceSpec, a many spec, or one with no target;
  • a parameter the target selector does not read, or, on a changelist action, one it does not read as an array;
  • on a changelist action, a parameter declaring a min_length of one or more: the page is declared with the selection bound to no row, since which rows are selected is known only on a request, and the kernel refuses a binding its parameter does not take. Selecting no row is then a page acting on none, rather than a refusal;
  • a page_kwargs key the mixin answers for;
  • anything the page's own as_view() refuses, under the admin's name for the action, BookAdmin['withdraw'], so the message says which declaration it is about.

docs.title: Confirming an operation
docs.text:
A spec with nothing for a person to fill in, served as the page that confirms it: what the operation acts on, and a button. Withdrawing a book, archiving a note, closing every stale ticket. Every argument the operation takes comes from the server's side - the route, a pool seed, a kwargs provider or server_arguments - so the page posts nothing but its token and the button, and nothing a post carries becomes an argument but the selection a bulk action names in posted_arguments.

SpecConfirmView serves a spec whose Validator is None. It shares everything with SpecFormView but the form: the admission, the target and its display, the affordances, the fragment wrapper under htmx, the post that does not commit, the success and its message. Each works as Serving a page describes it, and this page says only where the two differ.

from django_spec_html import SpecConfirmView

docs.title: Which view serves a spec
docs.text:
The spec's Validator The view a FormValidator SpecFormView: the page is the form None SpecConfirmView: the page is the target and a button any other neither: a page renders no inputs it would have to guess

Use SpecConfirmView when there is nothing to ask a person but yes. If the operation takes a value a person chooses - a reason, a date, a "yes, for good" box - declare a form that holds it and serve the spec with SpecFormView, whose asked_fields holds a confirmation back until the service asks for it. as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a spec with a Validator: a FormValidator's is pointed at SpecFormView, and any other is named.

The example withdraws a published book. The route names the book, and there is nothing else to send:

class IsSignedIn(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Sign in to withdraw a book."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated


@dataclasses.dataclass
class BookOut:
    """A book as the operation returns it, and as its page names it."""

    pk: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]  # another call's input: never shown
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]  # the name a page calls it by
    status: Status


def book_by_pk(*, pk: int) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.filter(pk=pk)


def withdraw(*, instance: Book) -> Book:
    instance.status = Status.DRAFT
    instance.save(update_fields=["status"])
    return instance


# No Validator: the route names the book, and there is nothing else to send.
withdraw_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=withdraw,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=book_by_pk,
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
    affordances=[
        Affordance(
            code="not_published",
            reason="Only a published book can be withdrawn.",
            when=Q(status=Status.PUBLISHED),
        )
    ],
)

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/withdraw/",
        SpecConfirmView.as_view(
            spec=withdraw_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_confirm_view.html",
            fragment_template_name="spec_confirm_view_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            # The parameter the route fills, which as_view() reads to know
            # that a post to this page needs to carry nothing.
            route_kwargs=("pk",),
            # BookOut describes the book withdrawn, so the page names it.
            display_target=True,
            commit_button="withdraw",
            success_message="Book withdrawn.",
        ),
    ),
    path("books/", books, name="books"),
]

docs.title: What the page renders
docs.text:
GET renders template_name with the context every page builds - view, spec, target, a set's target_count and target_counted_at, target_display on a page that sets display_target, and unavailable when an affordance is not met, or on a page serving actions unavailable_actions, refused_actions and action_buttons, each action's own answer - and no form. A key with nothing to hold is absent, as on every page, so a template's {% if form %} is false rather than {{ form }} rendering None. The template renders its own <form method="post">, the CSRF token and the submit button:

<div id="withdraw">
  {% if target_display %}<p>Withdraw <strong>{{ target_display.label }}</strong>?</p>{% endif %}
  {% if unavailable %}<p>{{ unavailable.reason }}</p>{% endif %}
  {% if requested_input %}<p class="asked">{{ requested_input.message }}</p>
  {% else %}{% for error in errors %}<p class="error">{{ error }}</p>{% endfor %}{% endif %}
  <form method="post" hx-post="" hx-target="#withdraw" hx-swap="outerHTML">{% csrf_token %}
    <button name="withdraw"{% if unavailable %} disabled{% endif %}>Withdraw it</button>
  </form>
</div>

The URLconf above renders it as the fragment under htmx, and inside this page otherwise:

<html><body><h1>Withdraw a book</h1>{% include "spec_confirm_view_form.html" %}</body></html>

Above, the page names the book by its LABEL. On a draft the button is disabled, with the affordance's reason above it. Dispatch still asks every affordance on the post, so a book withdrawn between the page and its post is refused at 409.

docs.title: The shipped template
docs.text:
A template is optional. A view naming none renders django_spec_html/spec_confirm.html, which this package ships, with its target pane and button in django_spec_html/spec_confirm_fragment.html, the file an htmx request is answered with. It is found, refused at as_view() when no engine finds it, and overridden as the form page's is: list django_spec_html in INSTALLED_APPS with APP_DIRS on. It renders, escaped and with no stylesheet, script or htmx attribute:

  • the target pane: a set's count and when it was counted, and target_display where the page sets display_target, but never the target itself;
  • an unmet affordance's reason, with the button disabled;
  • a refused post's errors as a list, or a question's message alone, since no control is built from its schema; a refusal's code is the form's data-code;
  • the button, posting commit_button's name where one is set.

docs.title: What a post sends
docs.text:
POST dispatches with the route's kwargs alone, read by route_kwargs and coerced by their declarations, with the request's seeds and the binding laid over them, as a form page's are. The post's own data is never read but for the names posted_arguments lists: not the CSRF token, not the button, not any other key named like a parameter. A post carrying pk=7 to /books/3/withdraw/ withdraws book 3. So the closed argument set holds with nothing to check, and a post cannot fill a parameter the route, a seed or server_arguments fills, nor one nobody declared.

commit_button works as on a form page: above, only a post carrying withdraw runs the operation, and any other post is the page again, with refreshed in its context. A page with actions takes no commit_button: as_view() refuses the pair, and an action keyed like a posted_arguments name or csrfmiddlewaretoken, which every post carries. Each action's button answers its own availability: the shipped template disables an unavailable action's button and shows its reason, the others stay usable, and a post naming the unavailable one is refused at 409, as on a form page. An action after the first that the user may not run - its permissions refuse them, or its scope check refuses the target - is disabled with no reason and no code, its key in refused_actions, and a post naming it is refused, 403 or 404, as before. A refused post's page keeps each action's state, asked of the target that post found, as on a form page.

docs.title: A bulk action over ticked rows
docs.text:
A list whose rows carry checkboxes and whose one button archives the ticked ones posts the selection itself: the rows are the person's choice, not the route's. posted_arguments names the parameters a post supplies, and nothing else the post carries is read. Here archive_notes_spec reads Parameter("ids", "array", items="integer") and archives those notes:

from django.urls import path, reverse_lazy

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "notes/archive/",
        SpecConfirmView.as_view(
            spec=archive_notes_spec,
            success_url=reverse_lazy("notes"),
            posted_arguments=("ids",),
        ),
        name="archive-notes",
    ),
]

The list renders a checkbox per row and a button that posts them with htmx's hx-include, so the boxes need no form of their own:

<table>
  {% for note in notes %}
    <tr><td><input type="checkbox" name="ids" value="{{ note.pk }}"></td><td>{{ note }}</td></tr>
  {% endfor %}
</table>
<button hx-post="{% url 'archive-notes' %}" hx-include="[name=ids]:checked"
        hx-headers='{"X-CSRFToken": "{{ csrf_token }}"}' name="archive">Archive</button>
  • Each name is read as a query string is, by the kernel's flat_arguments: every value of an array parameter, so ids=3&ids=5 is [3, 5], a comma list split (ids=3,5), the last value of anything else, and a blank absent, so a post with nothing ticked carries no ids. It is then merged with the route's arguments and coerced by its declaration.
  • Any other posted key never reaches the service, a parameter of the spec included, so the closed argument set stays closed.
  • A refused value is a refused post: ids=x answers 400 with "ids.0: Enter a whole number." in errors, as does a list the shape check refuses (too short for a min_length), or under refusal_redirect that message and a redirect back to the list. It is never a 404: route_refusal_404 is the route's alone.
  • as_view() checks the names: each must be a parameter of the spec, and none may be one route_kwargs fills from the URL, since a parameter is the route's or the post's, never both. posted_arguments must be a tuple.

docs.title: Every required parameter has a source
docs.text:
as_view() refuses a spec demanding a parameter that nothing but a post could supply, since no post to this page carries one unless posted_arguments names it. Which parameters the call demands is the kernel's answer, read through bind_arguments on a call carrying nothing: a parameter that is optional or declares a default is not demanded, and nor is a key a typed kwargs provider fills or may decline, or any read an untyped provider reaches. Each one left must be supplied by one of four sources, as they stand when the URLconf is imported:

Source Supplies the route each parameter route_kwargs names a kwarg into: a tuple's names, a mapping's targets the seeds each name the kernel's server_owned_keys reads off the declared pool_seeds, such as a reflected read a registered seed fills the binding each name server_arguments binds a value to the post each name posted_arguments lists

The route must say what it fills. as_view() is called while the URLconf is being built, before the pattern it is mounted on exists, so under the strict rule, route_kwargs = None, the route supplies nothing to this check. That is why the example names route_kwargs=("pk",). A mapping counts only the parameters it maps a kwarg into, so under {"org": None}, for an include() prefix, a pk the route still passes under its own name is not counted until it is mapped to itself: {"org": None, "pk": "pk"}. Without any:

SpecConfirmView requires pk, which no post to a confirmation carries: fill each from the route, naming it in route_kwargs, or from a pool seed, a kwargs provider or server_arguments, or name it in posted_arguments.

A seed only get_pool_seeds adds per request is not seen either, since there is no request yet: declare it on pool_seeds. A name server_arguments withholds is refused by the kernel's own check_server_arguments first, in its words.

docs.title: A refused post
docs.text:
A refused post is the confirmation page again, at the status of the one map, and needs no messages app: a button posted from another page lands on a page that works, and says why.

  • The page answers 400 for an argument refusal, 409 for a conflict or an unavailable action, 422 for any other service refusal, and under htmx the fragment at 200, as on every page.
  • The context carries errors, every message the refusal holds, as a list of strings in the refusal's order. With no field to put one on, a message about a parameter is prefixed with its path: with route_refusal_404 off, a route value the target's reads refuse is "pk: Enter a whole number." (on, it is Http404).
  • code is there for a refusal carrying one, as on a form page, and the target is shown again.
  • On a page serving actions, unavailable_actions, refused_actions, action_buttons and unavailable are there as GET puts them, asked of the target the post found, so a button GET disables stays disabled.
  • A denial is raised for the host's 403 or 404 page.

A confirmation's denial is the host's to answer, for htmx too, by the handlers in a denial under htmx.

docs.title: A refusal sent back
docs.text:
A button in a list's row is posted from the list, and the page a refusal is rendered on is one the person never opened. refusal_redirect=True sends the refusal back instead, to the page it came from. The URLconf routes the example as books/<int:pk>/withdraw/from-the-list/, with redirect_field_name="next" beside it, and a row's form posts to it with ?next= naming the page of the list it sits on:

urlpatterns += [
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/withdraw/from-the-list/",
        SpecConfirmView.as_view(
            spec=withdraw_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_confirm_view.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            route_kwargs=("pk",),
            commit_button="withdraw",
            # A row's button posts here with ?next=, the page of the list it
            # sits on, and both outcomes go back there: a success, and a
            # refusal, its reason sent as a message.
            redirect_field_name="next",
            refusal_redirect=True,
        ),
    ),
]
  • An invalid, a failed or a needs-input refusal is sent back. Each message the page would have shown in errors is sent through messages.error, and the refusal's code, where it has one, is the message's extra_tags, so the list can style or match an unavailable action: a book withdrawn already is sent back with "Only a published book can be withdrawn." tagged not_published.
  • The post redirects to get_refusal_url(refused): the safe URL redirect_field_name reads, checked as a form page checks it, and otherwise success_url. Override it to read the refusal, such as to send one code to a page of its own. Under htmx it answers HX-Redirect to the same URL, since an XHR would follow a 302 and swap the list into the row.
  • A denial is raised as ever, for the host's 403 or 404 page.
  • Without the messages middleware the page is rendered as above. Django raises MessageFailure with nowhere to keep a message, before any is stored, so the page renders the refusal itself rather than lose it in a redirect. A refusal with no message to send - an empty detail, or an empty message, which Django's storage drops - is the page again too.
  • A refusal sent back reads nothing for the page. The redirect is decided before the target is shown again, so a set is not counted and no presenter is asked.

as_view() refuses refusal_redirect on a page with no success_url that does not override get_refusal_url, since a refused post naming no safe URL would have nowhere to go. A form page has no such switch: a refused form redirected away would lose what the person typed.

docs.title: A success
docs.text:
A success redirects to get_success_url(result), or under htmx answers HX-Redirect or the spec-result fragment, as on a form page. Where the view names redirect_field_name, a safe URL the post or its query carries under that key is where the success goes instead, as on a form page: the example above returns to /books/?page=3. Nothing the post carries is an argument, so the key never reaches dispatch.

success_message is formatted with the target, % with a mapping whose one key is target, result.instance: "%(target)s was archived." names the row by its str(). A form page formats with the cleaned data, which with no Validator is {}. A set is the queryset, read when the message is formatted, so it holds the rows that still match once the operation has run. To name what the operation returned, override get_success_message(result) and read result.value. The message is sent where the messages middleware runs, and skipped where it does not.

docs.title: A question cannot be answered here
docs.text:
A service raising AdditionalInputRequired is shown its question, and the page cannot answer it. The schema is checked first by the kernel's check_requested_input, as on a form page. Then the page is re-rendered at 422, or as the fragment at 200, with requested_input - the message and the schema - and the message in errors.

The page builds no control from a schema, and no post is read for an answer, so a confirming post is asked again. With no Validator, an answer could only be a top-level parameter the spec reads, and reading one off the post would undo what the page is for:

  • every post carries the CSRF token and the button, so refusing undeclared keys needs a list of exemptions, and a box with no value posts "on", which a boolean parameter refuses;
  • the template would have to build the control from the schema, which no page does: on a form page, the form declares it;
  • and the post would become a channel filling a read on every post, not only the one a question asked.

So an operation that asks a person something mid-flight declares a form that holds the answer, an optional BooleanField, and is served by SpecFormView with that field in asked_fields, as the confirmation page shows. A page with a target and a button is already the confirmation: a service that also asks on this route will ask forever.

docs.title: Not a gate on an agent route
docs.text: Neither the page nor a question is a security boundary. The spec is one declaration for every route, and on an agent route the same AdditionalInputRequired goes back to the model as a retry naming the missing argument, which the model can answer confirmed: true itself on its next call, with nobody asked; the page's button is no gate there either, since an agent calls the operation without it. So nothing that must have a person's yes may rely on either. For a human gate on an agent route, enable ToolGuard in django-spec-agents, whose approval card a person answers before the tool runs, and keep the spec's tool out of its exempt list.

docs.title: Serving a formset
docs.text:
A many spec takes a list of rows under its many_argument, and the kernel validates the call per row: the shape check and the Validator run on each row, every failing row is refused at once, and each refusal is addressed by the row's index. SpecFormSetView serves one as a page: a formset of the spec's form, one form a row, posted as the list. The single-form page refuses a many spec, since one form posts one row; this is the page that serves it. The request's hooks, the htmx fragment, a post that does not commit and the denials are that page's own code; this page describes what differs, which is the form, the reading, the refusal, the scope check and the success message.

from django_spec_html import SpecFormSetView

The examples on this page add several books in one call. The spec's Validator is a FormValidator of a row's form, and the spec is many:

class BookRowForm(forms.Form):
    title = forms.CharField(max_length=100)
    price = forms.DecimalField(max_digits=6, decimal_places=2)
    author = forms.ModelChoiceField(queryset=Author.objects.all())


class IsSignedIn(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Sign in to add books."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated


def add_books(*, data: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> list[Book]:
    # ``data`` is a list: each row's cleaned data, in the order posted.
    return [Book.objects.create(**row) for row in data]


# A many spec: its rows travel as one list under ``items``, each validated by
# the form, and the service runs once for them all. At most five a call.
add_books_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_books,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(BookRowForm),
    many=True,
    many_max_length=5,
)

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/batch/",
        SpecFormSetView.as_view(
            spec=add_books_spec,
            template_name="spec_formset.html",
            fragment_template_name="spec_formset_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            # Three blank forms; a form left blank sends no row.
            extra=3,
            # "Save" runs the operation, and "Add a row" offers one more form.
            commit_button="save",
            add_button="add",
            success_message="%(count)d books were added.",
        ),
    ),
    path("books/", books, name="books"),
]

The template renders the formset inside a POST form with its token. Render {{ formset.management_form }} as well as the forms, or every post is refused, and {{ formset.non_form_errors }}, where a refusal of the list as a whole is placed:

<form method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">
  {% csrf_token %}{{ formset.management_form }}{{ formset.non_form_errors }}
  {% for form in formset %}<fieldset>{{ form }}</fieldset>{% endfor %}
  <button name="add">Add a row</button>
  <button name="save">Save</button>
</form>

A template is optional. A view naming none renders django_spec_html/spec_form_set.html, which this package ships, with its formset in django_spec_html/spec_form_set_fragment.html, the file an htmx request is answered with. It is found, refused at as_view() when no engine finds it, and overridden as the form page's is: list django_spec_html in INSTALLED_APPS with APP_DIRS on. It renders, escaped and with no stylesheet or script, the management form, the non-form errors - a question's message among them - and each form as a fieldset of its own with its errors, through django_spec_html/spec_form_set_row.html inside <div id="spec-form-set-rows">, then the submit button, posting commit_button's name where one is set, and the add_button, which skips the browser's checks, since its post commits nothing. The add button's htmx attributes, below, are its only ones, inert without htmx. It has no target pane: a many spec's rows are its forms.

docs.title: The formset
docs.text:
GET renders template_name with an unbound formset under formset, and view and spec beside it, once the principal is admitted: an anonymous visitor above gets Django's own PermissionDenied.

  • Admission asks the scope check of nothing. There is no target to look up, so after the spec's class-level check the page asks the scope check of None, as dispatch asks it of every many call, and a principal the post would refuse is never offered the page. A route value the spec's reads refuse is Http404, as on every page (route_refusal_404). A post asks it once: dispatch asks it, and where the page's own reading refuses the post first - its management form, a row's coercion - the page asks it before answering, so a principal it refuses is denied rather than shown the formset, as the single page denies one before reading its form. A route value the reads refuse leaves it unasked, as on the single page: there are no arguments to ask it with.

  • extra blank forms, 1 by default, after the spec's many_min_length forms, which a person must fill in. The page above offers three.

  • Never more forms than the spec takes. The formset's min_num and max_num are the spec's many_min_length and many_max_length, never attributes of the view, so no second declaration can drift from the first. The formset validates neither: the list's length is the kernel's to refuse, in its words. A Validator's formset_class is used as it is declared, its own extra, min_num and max_num with it, below.
  • Every form is built as the Validator builds a row's, with what its form_kwargs answers, through the kernel's form_keywords, as the single page builds its form: asked once per request, with the principal, the request's seeds and its call context. A many spec has no target to hand it, so the answer is the same for every row.
  • No target pane. A many spec's rows are its forms, so the context carries no target_display and display_target is refused at as_view(). A spec with no collection_selector_spec has no set either, and no target or target_count; a set edited puts both in the context.

docs.title: The post
docs.text:
Each form is read as the single page reads its form: through its own widgets, a blank field absent, a disabled field not read, a date in the form's input format sent in the form the shape check reads, and a choice's key coerced against the row's own declaration. The rows travel in the formset's order as one list under many_argument, and the service receives it once.

  • A form left as it came sends no row. An extra form a person did not touch is not sent, so the page above, posted with its middle form blank, adds two books, not three. The first many_min_length forms are sent however they are left, and the kernel refuses a blank row there as it refuses any row missing a required field.
  • The management form is never an argument. Its keys - TOTAL_FORMS, INITIAL_FORMS and the rest, under the formset's form- prefix - are the formset's own, as the CSRF token is the page's. A post missing them, or carrying ones Django refuses, is answered at 400 with Django's own message as a non-form error, and nothing is dispatched: a formset without its management form reads no forms, and would send an empty list.
  • The route's kwargs are the call's, read and coerced once beside the list, never inside a row, and checked against the spec's top level: a many spec's reads.

docs.title: A refused post
docs.text:
A refused post re-renders the formset at the status the single page answers it with, from the one map, and the refusal is split back onto the forms:

  • A refusal of row i lands on the form that sent it, through add_argument_errors, so a form left blank and dropped shifts nothing: on the page above, a bad price in the third form, posted beside a blank second one, is the list's row 1 and is placed on the third form.
  • A refusal of the list as a whole lands on the formset's non_form_errors(): its length - six books where the spec takes five - and a message the Validator gives about the rows together.
  • A refusal of a route value, with route_refusal_404 off, is a non-form error too, prefixed with its name, "shelf: Enter a whole number.", in the same post as the rows'.
  • Every row's own checks answer in the same post. Beside an InvalidArguments, each sent form is validated as the Validator validates a row's, so a row the shape check refused - a required field left blank - shows its form's further checks, a clean() among them, beside it. On a partial spec the forms carry the refusal alone, as a partial page's form does.
  • Any other refusal - a conflict, a service's own rule - is its message as a non-form error, and no form is validated again.

A question is answered by its message alone. An AdditionalInputRequired is checked by the kernel's check_requested_input first, as on every page, so a schema no route could hear answered - a key declared only inside a row among them - raises ImproperlyConfigured and is never rendered. Then the formset is re-rendered at 422 with the message as a non-form error and requested_input, its message and schema, in the context, with no fields. A many call's top level is the list and the spec's reads, which no form declares, and the page builds no widget from a schema, so a confirmation asked once for the whole call is not built on this page.

docs.title: Adding a row
docs.text:
add_button names a second submit button whose post is the page again with one more form, bound to everything posted, and nothing dispatched. It needs a commit_button, since without one every post commits, the add button's included. The page above names both: "Save" runs the operation, and "Add a row" offers a fourth blank form with the first three as they were filled in. At the spec's many_max_length it offers none, since the list takes no more. Every other post that does not commit is the page again with the forms it posted, validated by nothing, as on the single page.

Over htmx, the shipped add button appends one row. It carries hx-post, hx-target="#spec-form-set-rows" and hx-swap="beforeend", so a page that loads htmx posts the formset and is answered, at 200, with the new form alone, rendered by django_spec_html/spec_form_set_row.html, then the management form's TOTAL_FORMS input, one higher, with hx-swap-oob="true", which htmx swaps over the page's own. The new form is the formset's empty_form at the next index, built with the same form_kwargs as every other form. At many_max_length the answer is 204 with no body, and htmx swaps nothing. The answer is chosen by the request's HX-Target: an htmx add aimed anywhere else than spec-form-set-rows, such as a whole form posted with hx-swap="outerHTML" as in the template above, is the formset again with one more form, and so is an add without htmx. A project's own template that wants the row answer gives its rows that id and its add button that target, and overrides the row template as any shipped template is overridden.

docs.title: Editing a set
docs.text:
The page builds the Validator's own formset. A FormValidator declaring a formset_class validates the call's rows as that formset, its clean() among them, on every transport; the page renders the same class, so the rule over the whole set is declared once. A refusal from that clean() is the formset's non_form_errors(), as any refusal of the list as a whole is.

A model formset edits the spec's collection. A many spec may declare a collection_selector_spec, the set its rows edit, and a BaseModelFormSet as the Validator's formset_class edits it:

class OneTitleEach(forms.BaseModelFormSet):
    def clean(self) -> None:
        kept = [
            form.cleaned_data.get("title")
            for form in self.forms
            if not self._should_delete_form(form)
        ]
        if len(set(kept)) != len(kept):
            raise ValidationError("Two books share a title.")


CatalogueFormSet = forms.modelformset_factory(
    Book, formset=OneTitleEach, fields=["title", "price", "author"], can_delete=True, extra=1
)


def every_book() -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.all()


def edit_catalogue(*, data: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
    for row in data:
        book = row.pop("id")
        if row.pop("DELETE"):
            book.delete()
        elif book is None:
            Book.objects.create(**row)
        else:
            Book.objects.filter(pk=book.pk).update(**row)


edit_catalogue_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=edit_catalogue,
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    validator=FormValidator(CatalogueFormSet.form, formset_class=CatalogueFormSet),
    many=True,
    collection_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(kind=SelectorKind.LIST, selector=every_book),
)

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/edit/",
        SpecFormSetView.as_view(spec=edit_catalogue_spec, success_url=reverse_lazy("books")),
    ),
    path("books/", books, name="books"),
]
  • GET renders one prefilled form a row, the collection the selector resolves for the principal handed to the formset as queryset=, then the class's own extra blank forms. Each row's form carries its key as a hidden input and, under can_delete, a DELETE box; the management form's INITIAL_FORMS is the set's count.
  • A post sends each row's form whole, its key with it, and the service reads the rows the kernel cleaned: the key as its row for an update, None for a new row, and DELETE true for a row a person deleted, which is sent with its values rather than dropped. A row the post leaves out is left alone. A key outside the set is refused on its own form, an extra form's too where the row form declares the key.
  • An extra form with its DELETE box ticked sends no row, as Django's formset skips it, filled in or not.
  • A model formset needs the collection. as_view() refuses one on a spec with no collection_selector_spec, which would otherwise build every row of the model.

docs.title: A success
docs.text: A success redirects to success_url, or answers HX-Redirect or the result fragment to htmx, as on the single page, and a view naming redirect_field_name returns to the URL it reads, as the single page does. success_message is formatted with the rows' count, % with {"count": n}, so "%(count)d books were added." above says how many: the single page formats with the cleaned data, and a many call's is a list, which % with a name cannot read. Override get_success_message(result) to read the rows, under result.data, or what the operation returned, under result.value.

docs.title: What as_view() refuses
docs.text: When the URLconf is imported: a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator; a spec that is not many; a Validator's model formset on a spec with no collection_selector_spec; a view displaying its target; an extra that is not a non-negative int; an add_button that is not a button's name, is set without a commit_button, or is the commit_button; a redirect_field_name that is either button; and either button or the redirect_field_name named under the formset's form- prefix, which every post carries. Then every check the single page makes of the request's hooks. The view is sync only in this release.

docs.title: Serving over HTTP
docs.text:
django_spec_html.http serves an operation from a Django view with nothing between the request and dispatch: no API framework, no serializer, no router. A view reads the principal and the arguments off the request, dispatches, and answers the result or the refusal as JSON.

from django_spec_html import AsyncSpecView, SpecView, adispatch_request, dispatch_request

It is the plumbing, not the pages: a view here answers JSON to a script or a fetch(). A page a person reads, such as a spec's own form rendered and re-rendered with its refusal, is a page view. The pieces the entry points are built from are public so that such a view reads a request by the same rules: request_principal, route_arguments and add_argument_errors.

The examples on this page serve two specs, a list of the principal's notes and a rename of one, declared as any spec is:

@dataclass
class Rename:  # what the write takes
    title: str


@dataclass
class NoteOut:  # what both answer, per note
    id: int
    title: str


class IsSignedIn(PermissionCheck):
    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated


class IsOwner(IsSignedIn):
    message = "Only the note's owner may rename it."

    def has_object_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any, target: Any) -> bool:
        return target.owner_id == principal.pk


def notes_of(*, user: Any, search: str = "", ordering: str = "title") -> QuerySet[Note]:
    return Note.objects.filter(owner=user, title__icontains=search).order_by(ordering)


def rename(*, instance: Note, title: str) -> Note:
    instance.title = title
    instance.save(update_fields=["title"])
    return instance


list_notes_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=notes_of,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    reads=Parameters.of(
        Parameter("search", "string", help="Part of the title, in any case."),
        Parameter("ordering", "string", choices=["title", "-title"], default="title"),
    ),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
)

rename_note_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=rename,
    permissions=[IsOwner()],
    validator=DataclassValidator(Rename),
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=lambda *, pk: Note.objects.filter(pk=pk),  # the row, or none
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
)

docs.title: A function view
docs.text:
dispatch_request is the whole of what a hand-written view calls:

def rename_note(request: HttpRequest, pk: int) -> HttpResponse:
    return dispatch_request(rename_note_spec, request, url_kwargs={"pk": pk})


async def arename_note(request: HttpRequest, pk: int) -> HttpResponse:
    return await adispatch_request(rename_note_spec, request, url_kwargs={"pk": pk})

The route's pk is passed as url_kwargs and is an argument beside the body's title. It is merged last, so a body naming another pk cannot move the view off note pk.

It reads the principal and the arguments, dispatches with the grant, pool_seeds and unknown_arguments it is given, and answers. The route_kwargs and server_arguments it also takes are the route's kwargs a spec does not read and the values the server answers for. The call's context holds request, the request it was handed, and view, which is the view= a host's own view passes as itself and None where it passes nothing, so a spec callable naming either is handed it (what the request carries). SpecView and AsyncSpecView pass themselves. The spec's parameters are read with that same dict, so a Validator whose parameters declares call_context declares to the request's reader what it declares to dispatch. The kernel's own helpers called around the read take that dict too: apply_server_arguments checks each bound value against what the spec declares to this call, so a value that declaration refuses is the host's ImproperlyConfigured, and the asked-input check lets a service ask for a key the spec declares to this call alone. The views' as_view() checks of route_kwargs and server_arguments run with no request, and read the parameters with no context.

The answer:

  • A not-found result is 404, {"detail": "Not found."}.
  • A success is the presented value, bare, with no envelope around it. The status is the caller's success_status, or else 204 for a service with nothing to present and 200 for everything else. A 204 has no body. A service with nothing to present at any other status the caller names answers an empty body with no Content-Type, at that status. djangorestframework-services answers the same, except that where an output selector ran and found nothing it answers 204 whatever the caller named. Here the status stays the caller's: the caller named it, and an empty re-read already has a meaning, the value None. A read whose value is None (an allow_none retrieve that found nothing) answers null, since None is its value.
  • A file is the download, where the spec presents its result through the kernel's FilePresenter: a FileResponse of the bytes or the file object, or a StreamingHttpResponse for an iterable of bytes, with the presented content_type, Content-Disposition: attachment naming the file (RFC 5987 quoted for a name outside ASCII), and Content-Length wherever the size is known. The status is the caller's success_status, or 200. as_view() refuses a spec the kernel's file_output refuses: a file presented by a LIST selector spec, or by one declaring many, returns_many or rendered affordances, since a list of files has no answer.
  • A refusal of either family is error_response's answer. Anything else propagates, a configuration error included: it is wrong for every caller, so it belongs to the host's error handling rather than to one client's response.

adispatch_request does the same from an async view, through adispatch and apresent. It reads the request in an executor hop of its own, because touching request.user is a session query and Django refuses one on the event loop. A refusal asking for input is checked against the spec's parameters in a hop of its own too, because a Validator's parameters may query to declare what it takes.

docs.title: The class form
docs.text:
SpecView is one spec as a view, and every attribute can be passed to as_view() or set on a subclass: spec, success_status, unknown_arguments, pool_seeds, methods, route_kwargs and server_arguments. Two methods a subclass may override, get_pool_seeds(request) and get_server_arguments(request), are what the request carries to the call.

urlpatterns = [
    # A read answers GET and HEAD, and its query string is its arguments:
    # /notes/?search=draft&ordering=-title
    path("notes/", SpecView.as_view(spec=list_notes_spec)),
    # A write answers POST: the pk from the route, the title from the body.
    path("notes/<int:pk>/rename/", SpecView.as_view(spec=rename_note_spec)),
    # The same write as a PATCH, served from async code.
    path("notes/<int:pk>/", AsyncSpecView.as_view(spec=rename_note_spec, methods=["patch"])),
    # The function views above.
    path("notes/<int:pk>/rename-by-hand/", rename_note),
    path("notes/<int:pk>/arename-by-hand/", arename_note),
    # The view above: the team from the route, as a seed rather than an argument.
    path("teams/<slug:team>/notes/", TeamNotes.as_view()),
    # A host's own view, handing itself to the call as ``view``.
    path("my-notes/", MyNotes.as_view()),
]

The methods follow the spec. A SelectorSpec answers GET and HEAD, a ServiceSpec POST. methods replaces that with the ones it names, from GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, in either case. Any other method is Django's own 405, with an Allow header listing exactly the methods served, and OPTIONS is Django's own answer.

as_view() checks the configuration when the view is built, so a view with no spec, one naming a method it cannot serve, an async def hook, route_kwargs naming a parameter the spec does not declare, or a binding that cannot mean what it says, fails when the URLconf is imported rather than on its first request. What only a request can show is checked on each request: the route, under kwargs a spec does not read, and the hooks' answers, under what the request carries. The spec may be a declaration of another library's, a SpecSource: it is compiled there too, a declaration that does not compile is refused there, and its methods follow the spec it compiles to.

AsyncSpecView is the same view with every handler async, through adispatch_request. Django serves a class async only when all of its handlers are, which is why it is a class of its own rather than a setting.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
request_arguments reads them, by method and body:

Request Read from Coerced GET, HEAD the query string yes, with coerce_flat any other method, application/json body the body, which must be an object no any other method, form or multipart body the form fields, and a multipart body's uploads yes, with coerce_flat any other method, no body nothing - any other method, any other body refused, 415 -

A flat source is read by the declaration. An array parameter takes every value its key was sent with (?ids=1&ids=2), and anything else takes the last. An array of numbers, integers, booleans or decimal strings also reads a value holding commas as its elements, ?ids=1,2 as [1, 2] with the space around each part trimmed: a comma cannot be part of such a value, and it is the spelling a django-filter CSV filter advertises. A decimal element stays the string it spells, so ?pks=1,2 is ["1", "2"], every digit kept. Repeated keys and commas may mix, and an empty part (?ids=1,,2) is refused at its index as any malformed element is. A list longer than the array takes - its max_length, or 1000 by the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting, which is the kernel's and keeps its name - is refused whole at its name, a 400 rather than the 500 a database answers past its variable limit, and is never split further than one element past it: see how long a list may be. An array of strings is split the same way when it declares choices and none of them holds a comma, as a django-filter OrderingFilter's do: every element must be a choice, so ?o=title,-pk can only be ["title", "-pk"]. An array of strings with no choices, or with a choice holding a comma, is never split, since a comma can be part of a string, and an array declaring no items is not either. A blank value is absent unless "" is one the parameter can take: a plain string can, and a number, a boolean, a date, a decimal, or a string whose choices leave the blank out cannot. A flat wire has no other spelling of "left blank", and an empty ?count= or ?since= from a filter form is not a refusal to count or a malformed date. Django's csrfmiddlewaretoken is never an argument. Then coerce_flat types the strings, and leaves an undeclared key for the closed argument set to refuse under the caller's policy.

A JSON body is read as it is. Its values are not coerced here: a "5" sent for an integer is the shape check's to read, and it reads it as 5, as it reads one from any caller (see the shape check). A body that does not parse, or is not an object, is refused as InvalidArguments under non_field_errors. An empty body is no arguments.

A body in any other format is refused as UnsupportedMediaType, answered 415, rather than read as no arguments: a PATCH sent as text/plain or application/merge-patch+json to an operation whose parameters are all optional would otherwise run with nothing and answer success. A request with no body carries no arguments whatever its Content-Type says, so a fetch(url, {method: "POST"}) for an operation its route names is served.

Django parses a form body into request.POST for POST alone, so a PUT, PATCH or DELETE form is parsed here the same way rather than arriving empty. An upload is an argument, under the name its part carries, as each field is: the upload itself, Django's UploadedFile, for a parameter of type file, every upload under the name for an array, and the last of repeated ones for anything else. It replaces a field of the same name, since a browser sends a file input only as a file. A POST's uploads are Django's own request.FILES; those in a PUT, PATCH or DELETE body are parsed here with its fields, by Django's own parser from the request's stream, so a file part is streamed to the upload handlers and DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE bounds the fields alone, as it does for a POST. Like a POST, such a body is gone once parsed: reading request.body afterwards, or calling request_arguments on the request a second time, raises Django's RawPostDataException. The entry points here read the arguments once, so this reaches only code that reads the body after the view - a middleware, an audit log, an error reporter. Reading request.body before the view keeps the body, and the arguments are then parsed from it as often as they are asked for; that read is a whole-body read, so DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE bounds the whole body again, uploads included, and a larger one raises RequestDataTooBig. An upload under a name the spec does not declare reaches the closed argument set like any undeclared field, and is refused under REJECT; a file input left empty is no upload, so it is absent. Only a multipart body carries one. An optional file's clear checkbox is a field of the same body, attachment-clear=true, and is read as every flat boolean is: true, false, 1 or 0. A checkbox with no value attribute posts on, which is refused, so a page posting to a SpecView gives it value="true".

The URL kwargs are arguments too, merged last so the route wins a clash, as it does in djangorestframework-services. A client-supplied value must not move the route's scope: a POST to /notes/4/rename/ whose body says "pk": 9 renames note 4 or nothing. A path segment with no converter arrives as a string and goes through coerce_flat like a query value. Every URL kwarg is an argument, so the spec declares each one. A route capturing a kwarg its spec does not declare raises ImproperlyConfigured on the first request it serves, under either unknown_arguments policy: the mismatch is the host's, wrong for every request, and a 400 would tell the client it had sent something wrong. A host scoping by a kwarg its spec does not take says so with route_kwargs.

docs.title: Kwargs a spec does not read
docs.text:
An include() prefix such as teams/<team>/ reaches every view under it, including one whose spec reads no team. route_kwargs on either JSON view and on the page, or on dispatch_request and request_arguments, says which kwargs fill which parameters:

  • None, the default, is the strict rule above.
  • A mapping from a captured name to the parameter it fills, or to None to drop it: {"note": "pk", "team": None}. A kwarg the mapping does not mention is still held to the strict rule, so a typo in a route is still caught.
  • A tuple of names is an allow-list: each passes under its own name, and every other kwarg is dropped.

Each refusal is ImproperlyConfigured, as the strict rule's is. On a view, as_view() refuses a bare string (a TypeError), and a target or an allowed name the spec does not declare, when the URLconf is imported. Two kwargs filling one parameter are refused on the request that captures both, since a view mounted on two routes may capture one on each. A route kwarg is never one of the server's values, whatever it fills: the client's URL chose it, so a malformed one is the client's 400. Nor may it fill a name the server answers for: the route is the host's, so a route contradicting the host's own binding is refused, by as_view() where route_kwargs names the parameter and on the request where the route captures it, pointing at route_kwargs={name: None}, which drops it explicitly.

docs.title: The route on its own
docs.text:
route_arguments is that rule on its own, for a view that reads the rest of its arguments some other way, such as through a bound form's widgets. It returns the kwargs as a plain, uncoerced copy, or raises ImproperlyConfigured naming every one the spec does not declare, so the caller merges it last and types it in the same call as everything else, and one refusal carries every problem:

def form_arguments(posted: Mapping[str, Any], url_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    parameters = rename_note_spec.parameters()
    return coerce_flat(parameters, {**posted, **route_arguments(parameters, url_kwargs)})

Merging the route last is what makes it win a clash with a posted field of the same name, and the one coerce_flat call types both.

docs.title: The principal
docs.text:
The principal is request.user, anonymous included: the spec's permission check is what decides whether anonymous may act, so it is handed the anonymous user rather than being pre-empted.

A deactivated account is refused, as PrincipalUnavailable (403), before anything else is read. Django's ModelBackend never logs one in, but AllowAllUsersModelBackend and a project's own backend may, and a deactivated principal never acts, on HTTP or off it. dispatch refuses one by the same rule, so a hand-written view handing request.user to it is covered too; the entry points refuse first so that the request is never read.

request_principal is that reading, public, so a host's own view refuses by the same rule and before it reads anything else. It raises PrincipalUnavailable for a deactivated account and returns request.user otherwise. Reading request.user is a session query, so an async view calls it off the event loop, as adispatch_request does.

docs.title: What the request carries
docs.text:
Two hooks on both JSON views, and on the page, read the request before dispatch, each defaulting to the attribute of its name. Django builds one view instance per request, so either may read self.kwargs too:

class InTeam(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Only a member of the team may read its notes."

    # ``team`` is a seed, so every transport serving this spec seeds its own.
    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any, *, team: str) -> bool:
        return principal.groups.filter(name=team).exists()


team_notes_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=notes_of,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn(), InTeam()],
    reads=list_notes_spec.reads,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
)


class TeamNotes(SpecView):
    spec = team_notes_spec
    # The route's team is a seed, not an argument: drop it.
    route_kwargs = {"team": None}
    # The server chooses the order; a client's ?ordering= is dropped.
    server_arguments = ServerArguments(values={"ordering": "title"})

    def get_pool_seeds(self, request: HttpRequest) -> PoolSeeds:
        # What the request carries, never the request itself.
        return self.pool_seeds.extend(team=lambda: self.kwargs["team"])

    def get_server_arguments(self, request: HttpRequest) -> ServerArguments | None:
        # The value may vary per request; the name is the declared one.
        return ServerArguments(values={"ordering": "-title" if request.user.is_staff else "title"})

Every route under the teams/<team>/ prefix captures team, which the spec does not read as an argument: route_kwargs = {"team": None} drops it from the route's arguments, and every other kwarg is still held strict, while get_pool_seeds hands it to the call as a seed. The server chooses the order, so a client's ?ordering= is dropped. It is declared, so as_view() checks the name when the URLconf is imported, and get_server_arguments varies the value per request while the name stays the declared one.

  • get_pool_seeds(request) answers the seeds the call is resolved with, so a tenant, a locale or a team the request carries reaches a permission check, a selector or a Validator. Seed what the request carries, never the request itself. No request seed is registered, and none is needed to reach one: a spec callable naming request or view - a seed's resolver, a selector, a permission check, an affordance condition, a form_kwargs, the service - is handed this request, and the view serving it, read off the call's context. On a reader with no request, which is MCP, the agent tools, the CLI and a task, the same callable is handed None, so a spec reading request.team is written for one transport. A spec reading team is one definition every transport can seed, and the request reaches a callable with no hook at all:
def my_notes(*, request: HttpRequest | None) -> QuerySet[Note]:
    if request is None:
        return Note.objects.none()
    return Note.objects.filter(owner=request.user).order_by("title")


my_notes_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=my_notes,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
)


class MyNotes(View):
    def get(self, request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse:
        # Passing itself hands this view to a callable naming ``view``.
        return dispatch_request(my_notes_spec, request, view=self)
  • get_server_arguments(request) answers the kernel's ServerArguments: values the server answers for, which outrank whatever the client sent, and names it withholds, which are dropped. A client's value for a name it was never offered is never refused, however malformed: ?ordering=sideways here, or ?pk=abc for a bound integer, which is dropped before the query string is coerced. The declared server_arguments is checked by the kernel's check_server_arguments at as_view(), against the declared pool_seeds; the hook may vary the values per request, and each is checked on every call, but it binds and withholds the declared names exactly, or the request raises ImproperlyConfigured, since the check at as_view() never saw any other. A seed get_pool_seeds adds under a name the binding binds or withholds is refused the same way: declared in pool_seeds, the as_view() check would have refused the binding with it.

Both hooks are plain def, and as_view() refuses an async def one: neither is awaited. AsyncSpecView runs both in an executor hop of their own, so one reading request.user or a model never queries on the event loop. A host's own view passes the same values to dispatch_request as pool_seeds= and server_arguments=, and calls check_server_arguments once, when it is built.

docs.title: What a callable reads about the transport
docs.text:
Every context this package builds carries "html" under the kernel's TRANSPORT_KEY, and HTML_TRANSPORT, exported from the package root, is that plain string. The JSON views, dispatch_request, adispatch_request, the pages and the admin's offer of an action all build their context through the kernel's build_call_context, which writes the stamp last, so one call reads one value in every stage: the spec's parameters, the checks, the affordances, the form's keywords, the service and the presenter, and what asks the same callables ahead of the call (a list page's rows, the admin's offer of an action). A callable reads it with the kernel's call_transport, whose None is a call no transport made:

def notes_only_on_this_transport(*, call_context: Mapping[str, Any] | None) -> QuerySet[Note]:
    if call_transport(call_context) != HTML_TRANSPORT:
        return Note.objects.none()
    return Note.objects.order_by("title")


transport_notes_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=notes_only_on_this_transport,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(NoteOut),
)

The selector answers only where the stamp is this package's. Another transport stamps its own name, and a caller that built no context stamps none, so call_transport answers None there and the selector finds nothing.

The as_view() checks read a spec's declaration with no context at all, so call_transport is None there and "html" on every request, as request is (what the request carries).

The context also holds format and action, both None here: this package has neither. They are no call seeds, so a callable naming either is handed nothing from the context, as before; one reading call_context finds them as None where it found no key. The value has no seam on this package. What a host chooses is view=, which dispatch_request and adispatch_request take (a page passes itself), beside the request it reads; get_pool_seeds and get_server_arguments add seeds and bound values, never an entry of the context. A host that wants another value builds its own context through the kernel's build_call_context and calls the kernel's dispatch.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
error_response answers both families, with the statuses djangorestframework-services uses. Two bodies differ from its answer. A service's string or list detail, which DRF answers as a bare list and this as a field map under non_field_errors, so every 400 here has one shape. And an AdditionalInputRequired schema, which DRF reads as an error detail and so writes with every value a string ("minimum": "1"), and this writes as the JSON Schema it is:

Refusal Status Body InvalidArguments 400 the error tree ServiceValidationError 400 its detail, as a field map PermissionCheckDenied, NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable 403 {"detail": message} ServiceNotFound 404 {"detail": message} ActionUnavailable 409 {"detail": message, "code": code} ServiceConflict 409 {"detail": message} AdditionalInputRequired, with a schema 422 {"detail": message, "schema": schema} ServiceError 422 {"detail": message} UnsupportedMediaType 415 {"detail": message} DispatchError 400 {"detail": message}

A row is read top to bottom and the first match answers, so a subclass is matched before its base. Every 400 body is a field map: a ServiceValidationError's string or list detail goes under non_field_errors, where a message about the input as a whole sits in the tree too, and the tree's integer row keys are strings on the wire. Messages render in the active language, lazy ones included.

A schema no route could hear answered is not a 422. dispatch_request and adispatch_request pass an AdditionalInputRequired schema through check_requested_input before writing it: a schema naming a key the spec does not declare, a key the server fills, or a shape an MCP elicitation form cannot render, raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the key, as it does on every other route. The seeds the check reads are the request's own, so a seed get_pool_seeds(request) supplies counts as the server's, as it does to dispatch. error_response alone has no spec in hand and writes whatever it is given.

Never 401. A session has no challenge to answer, and a 401 tells a client to start an authentication flow it has no way to finish. An anonymous caller a permission check refuses is a 403, like any other refused principal.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
CSRF is the host's middleware, as it is for any Django view. Nothing in the package is exempted: a POST from a session-authenticated browser carries the token, in the X-CSRFToken header for a fetch() or in the form for an HTML form, and CsrfViewMiddleware refuses one that does not. A route that needs no token is the host's decision, and one line:

# A route a script calls, authenticated by the host's own middleware rather than
# a session cookie, so it has no CSRF token to send. Exempting it is the host's
# decision, and one line.
urlpatterns += [
    path("hooks/notes/<int:pk>/rename/", csrf_exempt(SpecView.as_view(spec=rename_note_spec))),
]

docs.title: A refusal, placed on a form
docs.text:
add_argument_errors places a refusal on a host's own bound form, for a page that re-renders the form it posted with what dispatch refused. It uses Django's public form.add_error, beside whatever errors the form carries:

  • A key naming one of the form's fields puts its messages on that field.
  • non_field_errors, and Django's own "__all__", go to the form's non-field errors.
  • Any other key - a URL kwarg such as pk, or a key a service chose - goes to the non-field errors prefixed with its path: "pk: Enter a whole number.". A nested tree is flattened with its path joined by dots, "books.1.title: This field is required.", since a form is flat. Below a field the path is an array's element index, which means nothing to a person reading one control, so it is dropped there.
  • Never a duplicate. A message the form already carries at the same place is not added again. The form validating the same post says what the kernel says - a FormValidator's refusal is the form's own errors, and the shape check spells its messages as Django's fields do - so without this most refusals would show twice.
  • A form not yet validated is validated first, as reading form.errors would, so its own errors are the ones compared against, but with the guards a FormValidator's form is validated with. Its own validation would hand the database driver a number no integer column holds - a model choice field's key, a ModelForm's integer - which SQLite's refuses with OverflowError. Such a key is refused as invalid_choice and such an integer as max_value or min_value, in the words a FormValidator refuses them with, so the refusal of one is placed once. A form already validated is compared as it stands.

docs.title: Serving a page
docs.text:
A spec served as a server-rendered page: the form that validates a post is the form the page renders, every page works as a plain form post, and a refused post comes back as the page again with the refusal placed on its form. The statuses a refused post answers are the JSON views', so a client reading one reads the other the same way. An htmx request to the same URL gets the part of the page it swaps, from the same template.

SpecFormView serves a spec whose Validator is a FormValidator as the page a person fills that form in on: the form that validates the arguments is the form the page renders.

from django_spec_html import SpecFormView

The examples on this page serve a book's form, a plain Django form read as the spec's Validator:

class BookForm(forms.Form):
    title = forms.CharField(max_length=100, help_text="As printed on the cover.")
    price = forms.DecimalField(max_digits=6, decimal_places=2)
    status = forms.ChoiceField(choices=Status.choices)
    published_on = forms.DateField(required=False)
    author = forms.ModelChoiceField(queryset=Author.objects.all())
    shelves = forms.MultipleChoiceField(
        choices=[("fiction", "Fiction"), ("poetry", "Poetry")], required=False
    )

    def clean(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        cleaned = super().clean() or {}
        if cleaned.get("status") == Status.PUBLISHED and not cleaned.get("published_on"):
            raise forms.ValidationError("A published book needs its publication date.")
        return cleaned


# The form is read here, once: a field with no JSON type fails on this line.
book_validator = FormValidator(BookForm)

class IsSignedIn(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Sign in to add a book."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any) -> bool:
        return principal.is_authenticated


def add_book(*, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Book:
    # data is the form's cleaned_data; shelves is no column of the book's.
    columns = ("title", "price", "status", "published_on", "author")
    return Book.objects.create(**{name: data[name] for name in columns})


# BookForm, from the forms adapter's page, is the Validator and the page's form.
add_book_spec = ServiceSpec(service=add_book, permissions=[IsSignedIn()], validator=book_validator)
