The service is handed the form's cleaned_data as data: a Decimal price, a date and the Author row, not the strings a post carried. shelves is the form's own field and no column of the book, so the service stores only the columns it names.

class AddBookThenShowIt(SpecFormView):
    spec = add_book_spec
    template_name = "spec_form.html"

    def get_success_url(self, result: DispatchResult) -> str:
        # The row the service created, which no static success_url can name.
        return reverse("book", kwargs={"pk": result.value.pk})


urlpatterns = [
    # No template_name: the page is the one this package ships.
    path("books/new/", SpecFormView.as_view(spec=add_book_spec, success_url=reverse_lazy("books"))),
    path("books/add/", AddBookThenShowIt.as_view()),
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/edit/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=edit_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            # Linked from a page of the list as ?next=/books/?page=3, a save
            # returns to that page rather than the first.
            redirect_field_name="next",
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/change/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=change_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "books/shelve/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=shelve_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/withdraw/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=withdraw_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_target.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            # BookOut describes the book withdrawn, so the page shows it.
            display_target=True,
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "books/publish-drafts/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=publish_drafts_spec,
            template_name="spec_target.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            display_target=True,
            target_display_limit=3,
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "books/discard-drafts/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=discard_drafts_spec,
            template_name="spec_confirm.html",
            fragment_template_name="spec_confirm_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            display_target=True,
            asked_fields=("confirmed",),
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "books/discard-drafts/in-a-dialog/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=discard_drafts_spec,
            template_name="spec_confirm_dialog.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            display_target=True,
            asked_fields=("confirmed",),
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "editions/new/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=add_edition_spec,
            template_name="spec_edition.html",
            fragment_template_name="spec_edition_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            # Only "Add the edition" runs the operation: the author picker
            # and "Show their books" post the form to re-render it.
            commit_button="add",
            success_message="Edition %(number)s added.",
        ),
    ),
    path(
        "editions/new/checked/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=check_edition_spec,
            template_name="spec_edition.html",
            fragment_template_name="spec_edition_form.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            commit_button="add",
            # Every post that does not commit shows what "Add" would refuse,
            # a field's own request that field's errors alone.
            validate_on_refresh=True,
        ),
    ),
    path("branches/<branch>/books/new/", StockBook.as_view()),
    path("books/", books, name="books"),
    path("books/<int:pk>/", book, name="book"),
]

docs.title: The page's template
docs.text:
A template is optional. The first route above names none, so it renders django_spec_html/spec_form.html, the page this package ships, which is the default template_name. The shipped templates are found as any app's are, so a project rendering them lists the package as an app, with APP_DIRS on:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django_spec_html",
]

as_view() refuses a page rendering a shipped template that the view's template_engine does not find, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the template and the setting, so the URLconf's import says so rather than the first request's TemplateDoesNotExist. It asks for the page and its fragment, or the page alone where fragment_template_name names a fragment of the project's own or get_fragment_template_names is overridden, and follows neither one's extends or include: a shipped page copied into a directory of the project's own, without the app, needs base.html and target.html found there too. A page naming a template of its own needs no app.

The shipped page is a plain document: no stylesheet, no script, and no htmx attribute. Everything it shows is escaped. It renders:

  • the target pane: a set's count and when it was counted, and the target's display where the page sets display_target. Never the target itself, whose str() may be anything its model returns;
  • an unmet affordance's reason, with the form disabled, and its code as the paragraph's data-code;
  • on a partial page, a line saying a field left blank is left as it is. The form renders no HTML required there, as every partial page's form does;
  • the form, through form.as_div: its non-field and field errors, and on a confirmation page the question's message and the field it asks for, each once. A refusal's code is the form's data-code, and a form holding a file field posts as multipart/form-data;
  • the submit button, posting commit_button's name where one is set, so a post that does not commit is one made without it.

Its form is a file of its own, django_spec_html/spec_form_fragment.html, which the page includes and an htmx request is answered with, on every Django: a {% partialdef %} would not parse below Django 6.0 without django-template-partials configured. It defines no spec-result, so a success under htmx is HX-Redirect, as the page's is a redirect.

Overriding it is the Django way. A file of the same name in a template directory the engine searches first replaces the shipped one: django_spec_html/base.html, the document every shipped page extends, to put all three inside a project's layout, filling its title and content blocks; the page; or its fragment, to change the form. Or set template_name, and the page is a template of the project's own, any template that renders the form inside a POST form with its token. Every other route above does, and its template is as small as that:

<form method="post">{% csrf_token %}{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button></form>

A page of the project's own carries its form for htmx as its own spec-form fragment, below; a project overriding a shipped page keeps the shipped fragment.

GET renders template_name with an unbound form under form, and view and spec beside it: the names Django's FormView uses, with extra_context merged in as Django's ContextMixin does. The spec's class-level permission check runs first, so the page is never offered to a principal the post would refuse: an anonymous visitor above gets Django's own PermissionDenied, which the host's 403 page answers.

An update's page shows the row it updates. Every GET then finds its target as dispatch would, through resolve_target on the route's kwargs, coerced as a post's are: the row or set a target selector resolves, or None for a create.

  • A check refusing it - the object-level check on a row, the scope check on a set or on None - raises PermissionDenied, as the post would be refused; a missing row, or a selector's ServiceNotFound, is Http404; and so is a route value the spec's parameters refuse (route_refusal_404).
  • The form stays unbound, and shows the row's values for its own fields. A ModelForm of the row's model is built on a copy of the row, as the FormValidator binds it, so its own __init__ sees the row it edits. Any other form takes the row's values for the fields it names as its initial, and a field no model field matches keeps its own, as does a disabled one, which the post cleans from that initial rather than reading.
  • So a file the row holds is shown, linked, with the clear checkbox an optional file's ClearableFileInput offers beside it.
  • A create, a collection target and a missing row the instance selector's allow_none lets through show an empty form.
def book_by_pk(*, pk: int) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.filter(pk=pk)


def edit_book(*, instance: Book, data: dict[str, Any]) -> ChangeResult[Book]:
    return update_from_input(instance, data, exclude_fields=["shelves"])


# The same form behind an update: GET finds the book the route names, and the
# page shows its values for the form's fields.
edit_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=edit_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=book_validator,
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=book_by_pk,
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
)

The URLconf above routes it as books/<int:pk>/edit/.

POST starts as GET does: the route first, then the same check, and only then is the form built from the post. A refused post is answered with the page again, and dispatch's shape check comes before its own permission check, so without it a principal the spec refuses would be shown the page - every row a choice field lists, and extra_context - by posting a malformed form, and a form whose constructor reads rows would read them for that principal. The Grant the check returns goes to dispatch, so it runs once.

Then the post finds its target, as the page does, before the form is built or read. So the form a refused post re-renders is built on the row as the page's was, and shows its held file and the clear checkbox beside it. And the target answers before the shape check: a principal the object-level or scope check refuses is PermissionDenied, and a missing row Http404, even for a post that is malformed, where dispatch's own order would refuse the malformed post first and re-render the page for them. Dispatch is handed the target and the grant resolve_target returns, so it looks nothing up again and asks no check twice, and the request's CallSeeds, so the service runs on the values of the seeds the class-level check and the object-level or scope check were offered (one resolution per request). A route value the spec's parameters refuse is Http404 before the form is built. With route_refusal_404 off it is left to dispatch, and comes back in dispatch's one refusal beside the form's own, as a non-field error. A create resolves None and a collection target its set, each handed on the same way.

POST then binds the form to the post and reads the arguments through the form's own widgets, which is how Django reads a form:

  • A checkbox is True or False and a multi-select a list, where a flat reading would refuse a checkbox's "on". Only the form's fields are read, so the CSRF token and a named submit button never become arguments, and a disabled field is not read at all, since the form ignores what is posted for it.
  • A field left blank is absent, for every field, as it is to the form. An optional date, number or choice left empty is simply not sent, and a required field left empty is refused with "This field is required.", once.
  • A number, a date or a date-time in one of the field's input formats - 10/25/1974, a localized 12,50, 5.0 for an integer - is read by the field's own to_python and sent on in the form the shape check reads: an ISO date, an ISO date-time with its offset, a decimal string, a number. So the shape check never refuses what the form accepts. A value the field refuses is sent on as it came, and refused in the kernel's words, which are the field's own.
  • A ticked clear checkbox is read by its file's widget, which answers False, and is sent on as the argument the Validator declares for it, attachment-clear, so the file is cleared. Ticked beside an upload, both are sent, and the form refuses the pair in its own words.
  • The URL kwargs are merged last, so the route wins a clash, and typed with coerce_flat in the same call as everything else: one refusal carries every problem. Each is an argument, so the spec declares each one. A kwarg the route captures and the spec does not declare is the host's misconfiguration, wrong for every caller, so it raises ImproperlyConfigured under either unknown_arguments policy - the policy governs what a client sends - rather than blaming the client with a refused post.

Then dispatch. A success redirects to get_success_url(result), which resolves success_url as Django's redirect() does, so a path, a reverse_lazy or a URL name all work. Override it to read the result, as AddBookThenShowIt does to reach the book it created. A view that names redirect_field_name goes instead to the URL the request carries under that key, where it is safe: see returning where the page was opened from. A refusal ends in one of four outcomes, read from the same map as its status, and each is answered as the page or, for htmx, as the fragment:

Refusal Outcome The page answers The fragment answers InvalidArguments, ServiceValidationError invalid 400, the form re-rendered 200, the form fragment re-rendered UnsupportedMediaType invalid 415, the form re-rendered 200, the form fragment re-rendered AdditionalInputRequired needs_input 422, the form re-rendered 200, the form fragment re-rendered ActionUnavailable, ServiceConflict failed 409, the form re-rendered 200, the form fragment re-rendered ServiceError failed 422, the form re-rendered 200, the form fragment re-rendered DispatchError failed 400, the form re-rendered 200, the form fragment re-rendered PermissionCheckDenied, NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable denied PermissionDenied PermissionDenied ServiceNotFound denied Http404 Http404

A not-found result is Http404 too, in both. The outcome column is the package's Outcome, by value; a success is ok.

The first two rows place the refusal on the form, and a service's string or list detail is about the whole form. Every other re-rendered refusal is its message, among the form's non-field errors. An AdditionalInputRequired reveals the field that answers it as well, as the confirmation page.

A refusal of the arguments shows every error in one post. Beside an InvalidArguments, the page's own form - built as the Validator's is, with the same keywords - is validated too, and the refusal is placed beside what it found, never twice. So after a shape-check refusal - a required field left blank, a date that does not parse - the form's further checks, such as a length, clean() or uniqueness, answer in the same post rather than the next one: a book posted as published with no title and no date is told both. The page's form is validated as the Validator validates its own, under the kernel's clean_held_to_their_columns, so a value no column holds - a key past 64 bits - is refused in the field's own words and never reaches the database driver, whose SQLite raises OverflowError for it. With route_refusal_404 off, a post whose route value the target's reads refuse never found its row, so its form is not judged as one, and carries the refusal alone. Any other refusal - a conflict, a service's own rule, an unavailable action - is no verdict on the arguments, and the re-rendered form carries it alone. The statuses are error_response's, so a client reading a refused post - Turbo, which will not render a failed post answered 200 - reads its outcome from the status.

docs.title: A form that takes keywords
docs.text:
A form whose __init__ takes a keyword of its own - a queryset scoped by the principal or by a tenant - is handed it by the FormValidator's form_kwargs, and the page builds its own form with the same answer, through the kernel's form_keywords: the same principal, the request's seeds, the row the post acts on (the row itself, never the copy a ModelForm edits) and one call context per request, the very dict dispatch is then handed. On GET, on a refused post and for the post's own validation, the page's form is the Validator's, so the page offers the choices the Validator accepts:

class OfferedAuthorsForm(BookForm):
    """``BookForm``, offering the authors its constructor is handed."""

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, authors: QuerySet[Author], **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.fields["author"].queryset = authors


def offered_authors(*, user: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # Staff add a book by anyone; everyone else by an author already shelved.
    authors = Author.objects.all()
    if not user.is_staff:
        authors = authors.filter(books__isnull=False).distinct()
    return {"authors": authors}


shelve_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(OfferedAuthorsForm, form_kwargs=offered_authors),
)

The URLconf routes it as books/shelve/. A signed-in user who is not staff is offered only the authors already on the shelves, and a post naming another is refused on the author field; staff are offered every author.

docs.title: A form over any Validator
docs.text:
A spec validated by a DataclassValidator, a PydanticValidator or any other Validator is served by naming the form the page renders, form_class:

@dataclasses.dataclass
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int | None = None


class BookForm(forms.Form):
    title = forms.CharField()
    pages = forms.IntegerField(required=False)


SpecFormView.as_view(spec=add_book_spec, form_class=BookForm, success_url=reverse_lazy("books"))

The form renders and reads; the Validator alone decides. GET builds the form as it builds a FormValidator's, a row's values shown. A post is read off the form's fields as it always is, through each field's widget, merged with the route, coerced by the spec's parameters and dispatched: the Validator receives the values as posted, never the form's cleaned_data. The form is never validated. Its clean(), its field validators and a ModelForm's uniqueness queries never run, and a refused post's form carries the Validator's refusal and nothing else, each error on its field. A validate_on_refresh refresh follows the same rule.

The form's keywords are the view's. get_form_kwargs() answers what the form's __init__ is handed beside the post, on GET and on every post; it is empty by default, and it may not return data, files or instance, which the page sets. A FormValidator page keeps its Validator's form_kwargs.

success_message reads the Validator's data: % with it where it is a mapping, and otherwise with its attributes, so "%(title)s added" reads a dataclass's or a pydantic model's title.

as_view() holds the form to the spec, refusing, by the page and the field:

  • a form the post cannot be read off, as FormValidator(form_class) refuses it: a JSONField, a MultiValueField such as SplitDateTimeField;
  • an enabled field, or the <name>-clear checkbox an optional ClearableFileInput adds, that the spec's parameters do not declare: a file field over a Validator declaring no clear checkbox takes a plain FileInput;
  • a required parameter the form does not post, where neither the server (server_owned_keys, server_arguments) nor the route fills it. Only a tuple route_kwargs closes the route; under None or a mapping any parameter may come from the URL, and dispatch refuses one nobody sent. An optional parameter the form leaves out is allowed;
  • a field whose type disagrees with its parameter's: the same type, the same element type for an array, and the same format where the parameter declares one. The rule is exact, so an IntegerField over a number parameter is refused; write a FloatField. A parameter of type any takes any field;
  • a field whose required differs from its parameter's, either way;
  • a Validator naming any field in unsendable, which no form can post;
  • form_class over a FormValidator, whose form is already the page's;
  • a form defining its own clean() or clean_<field>(), a rule the page would silently not run: it belongs in the Validator. Django's own are allowed.

Choices, lengths, bounds and nullable are not compared: the Validator refuses at the post, in its own words. Under actions, every action shares the page's form_class, over any Validator but a FormValidator, and each is checked as above.

docs.title: A partial page
docs.text:
A partial spec gets the same page, built on the same form. The page's form renders no HTML required attribute, so the browser sends a post that leaves a field blank, and a blank field is absent, as it is on every page: on a partial call, a field the operation leaves as it is. A post with every field blank dispatches with no arguments but what a checkbox or a multi-select always sends, and the page does not refuse it.

# The same update as a partial one: a field left blank is left as it is.
change_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=edit_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=book_validator,
    instance_selector_spec=edit_book_spec.instance_selector_spec,
    partial=True,
)

The URLconf routes it as books/<int:pk>/change/: a post with the title left blank and a new price changes the price and keeps the title.

A blank field cannot clear a value there, since blank means "leave it": a partial operation that clears a value needs a field of its own that says so, as an optional file's clear checkbox does. A checkbox and a multi-select are always sent, ticked or not, so each is written as posted. And beside a shape-check refusal, a partial page's form carries the refusal alone: its Validator takes the fields a post leaves out off its own form, and the page's form, validated whole, would call each blank field required.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a view with no ServiceSpec, a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator, a many spec, whose list of rows no form posts, and a view with neither a success_url nor its own get_success_url; then every check the JSON views make of the request's hooks, below. The view is sync only in this release.

docs.title: What the page acts on
docs.text:
The page shows its target, the row or set the operation acts on, in the context beside the form, on GET and on every refused post it re-renders, the fragment included:

Key Holds Present target the row an instance_selector_spec found, or the set a collection_selector_spec resolved wherever there is a target: absent for a create, and for a missing row allow_none lets through target_count how many rows the set holds for a set target_counted_at when it counted them, django.utils.timezone.now() for a set target_display the target as a person reads it, below on a page that sets display_target

A key with nothing to hold is absent rather than None, as unavailable is.

@dataclasses.dataclass
class BookOut:
    """A book as an operation returns it, and as its page names it."""

    pk: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]  # another call's input: never shown
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    price: Decimal
    status: Status
    published_on: Annotated[datetime.date | None, FieldMarking.hidden()]


class WithdrawForm(forms.Form):
    reason = forms.CharField(max_length=200)


def withdraw(*, instance: Book, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Book:
    instance.status = Status.DRAFT
    instance.save(update_fields=["status"])
    return instance


# One book: the page shows it, by its title, beside the form.
withdraw_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=withdraw,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(WithdrawForm),
    instance_selector_spec=edit_book_spec.instance_selector_spec,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
)


class PublishForm(forms.Form):
    published_on = forms.DateField()


def drafts() -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.filter(status=Status.DRAFT).order_by("title")


def publish(*, collection: QuerySet[Book], data: dict[str, Any]) -> list[int]:
    published = list(collection.values_list("pk", flat=True))
    collection.update(status=Status.PUBLISHED, published_on=data["published_on"])
    return published


# Every draft at once: the page counts the set, and names the first few.
publish_drafts_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=publish,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(PublishForm),
    collection_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(kind=SelectorKind.LIST, selector=drafts),
    output_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=lambda *, result: Book.objects.filter(pk__in=result).order_by("title"),
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
    ),
)

BookOut marks its fields for the display below: pk is a handle, another call's input and never shown; title is the label, the name a page calls the row by; status is spoken as its display, "Draft" rather than draft; and published_on is hidden.

The URLconf routes the first as books/<int:pk>/withdraw/ and the second as books/publish-drafts/, with target_display_limit=3, both with display_target=True and both rendering this template:

{% if target_count is not None %}
  <p>{{ target_count }} book{{ target_count|pluralize }} selected, counted at {{ target_counted_at|time:"H:i" }}.</p>
  {% if target_display %}
    <ul>{% for book in target_display %}<li>{{ book.label }}</li>{% endfor %}</ul>
    {% if target_count > target_display|length %}<p>The first {{ target_display|length }} are shown.</p>{% endif %}
  {% endif %}
{% elif target_display %}
  <h1>{{ target_display.label }}</h1>
  <dl>{% for name, value in target_display.pairs %}<dt>{{ name }}</dt><dd>{{ value }}</dd>{% endfor %}</dl>
{% endif %}
<form method="post">{% csrf_token %}{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button></form>

docs.title: A bulk page
docs.text:
A spec with a collection_selector_spec acts on a set, and its page says how many rows the set holds. An empty set is no refusal: its scope check is still asked, there is no not-found exit, and the page above says "0 books selected" where an instance page answers 404. A queryset is counted with a COUNT on a fresh clone of it, so no row is read to count it; a set a selector answers as a list is counted with len().

The count is a time-of-check, not a promise. The rows may change between the page and its post, so the context carries when the set was counted, and a template says "5 books selected, counted at 14:02" rather than "5 books will be published". The post does not replay what the page counted: it re-runs the service on the set it finds then, and a refused post counts the set again. A successful post counts nothing. So nothing about the count belongs in a hidden input.

A set the person ticks is posted, not selected. A list whose checkboxes choose the rows a button acts on serves the action with SpecConfirmView and its posted_arguments, which read the ticked ids off the post that hx-include sends: the recipe is a bulk action over ticked rows.

docs.title: The target's display
docs.text:
A page that sets display_target = True shows its target as a person reads it, under target_display. It is off by default, because the FieldMarkings it reads are on the spec's Output - its own presenter's, or its output_selector_spec's - and an Output describes what the operation returns, which need not be its target: a withdrawal may return a receipt. A page whose Output is marked serves as it did until it opts in, and asks no presenter. On:

  • the target is presented through that presenter, handed the context dispatch hands it: the principal, the target, the request's one call context, and the call's seeds as ambient;
  • then projected by the kernel's project_payload: a HIDDEN field is dropped, and a choice is spoken as its display;
  • and every HANDLE is dropped as well, at any depth. An agent keeps a handle to pass to another tool, and a person is never shown one.

A row's display is a dict: its fields, the same fields as pairs of name and value in order, and label, the value of the field marked LABEL, where one is. Loop over pairs rather than fields.items: a template looks the key items up before the method, so an Output with a field of that name would loop over its value. Above, the book is named "The Lathe of Heaven" and its fields are its title, its price and its status, read as "Published": the key is a handle and the publication date is hidden. A set's display is a list of those, one per row, for at most target_display_limit rows, 10 by default: the first that many in the set's own order, read by one query bounded by a LIMIT, and presented by one call of the presenter's presented_rows(). target_count still counts every row, so a template can say how many it left out. as_view() refuses a target_display_limit that is not a positive int, a bool included.

as_view() refuses a page displaying its target, when the URLconf is imported, where its spec has no Output, where the Output marks none of its own fields - choices alone are not markings, and nor is a marking only inside a nested object - and where the kernel's projection refuses the markings, such as two fields marked LABEL. What it cannot check is whether the Output describes the target's rows, since that is known only once one is presented: an Output that does not raises on the page's first request. That is the cost of turning the display on. A bulk operation whose service returns something else re-reads its rows with an output_selector_spec, as publish_drafts_spec does. The raw target stays beside the display, for a template that wants both.

docs.title: The confirmation page
docs.text:
A service that finds it needs one more value asks for it by raising AdditionalInputRequired with a schema keyed by the argument it wants back, and the page renders that question: the form again, bound to every value the post carried, with the field that answers it revealed. The answer comes back as an ordinary field of the next post, so there is nothing to hold between the two and no session to resume.

class DiscardForm(forms.Form):
    reason = forms.CharField(max_length=200, required=False)
    # The answer to the service's question, declared like any other field:
    # the page holds it back until the question asks for it.
    confirmed = forms.BooleanField(required=False, label="Yes, discard them")


def discard(*, collection: QuerySet[Book], data: dict[str, Any]) -> list[int]:
    if not data["confirmed"]:
        raise AdditionalInputRequired(
            f"{collection.count()} drafts will be deleted. Confirm to proceed.",
            schema={"confirmed": {"type": "boolean"}},
        )
    discarded = list(collection.values_list("pk", flat=True))
    collection.delete()
    return discarded


# Every draft, deleted once a person says yes.
discard_drafts_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=discard,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(DiscardForm),
    collection_selector_spec=publish_drafts_spec.collection_selector_spec,
    output_selector_spec=publish_drafts_spec.output_selector_spec,
)

The answer is a field the spec's form declares, here confirmed: an optional BooleanField, whose box left unticked cleans to False. The page builds no widget from the schema, because the closed argument set refuses a key no parameter declares, so a control the form does not declare could never carry the answer. asked_fields holds the field back until a question names it. It is taken out of the form every GET and every other refusal renders, so {{ form }}, or a template rendering fields one by one, shows no box, and a box never shown posts nothing: the service reads False and asks. as_view() refuses asked_fields unless it is a tuple of the form's own fields, each optional, since a field held back is absent from every post no question asked for, none the form disables, since a disabled field is never read from a post, and none a server_arguments binding answers for. A held field a refusal's error names is shown with its error.

The URLconf routes it as books/discard-drafts/, with display_target=True and asked_fields=("confirmed",), through this template and a page that includes it, named as the fragment_template_name:

<form method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">{% csrf_token %}
  <p>{{ target_count }} draft{{ target_count|pluralize }} selected, counted at {{ target_counted_at|time:"H:i" }}.</p>
  <ul>{% for book in target_display %}<li>{{ book.label }}</li>{% endfor %}</ul>
  {{ form }}
  <button name="save">{% if requested_input %}Discard them{% else %}Discard{% endif %}</button>
</form>

What a post that is asked gets back:

  • The kernel's check_requested_input reads the schema first, with the request's seeds. A question no route could hear answered - a key no parameter declares, one a seed fills, a shape a transport cannot render, a type the parameter would refuse - raises ImproperlyConfigured out of the view, on the page and in the fragment alike, rather than being rendered. It is the service's mistake, and the JSON views raise it too.
  • The page answers 422, the map's status, and the fragment 200, in place: the form's own target, with no HX-Retarget or HX-Reswap.
  • The form is re-rendered with the boxes the schema names revealed, every other value as it was posted, and the message among its non-field errors, as any other refusal's. A box asked for again after a yes is shown empty, so one click never answers a question nobody read.
  • The context carries requested_input, absent on every other answer:
Key Holds requested_input.message the refusal's message requested_input.schema the schema it asked under, or None requested_input.fields the form's bound fields the schema names, in its order

A key the schema names that no field of the form declares, such as a parameter the spec reads from the route, is asked by its message alone.

The page that asks counts again. On a bulk page the set is counted for the post that asked, after the service's pass, so target_count and target_counted_at say what the confirming post will find as of then, not what the GET counted: above, a draft added between the page and its post makes the question say "3 drafts". The confirming post re-runs the service on the set as it is when it arrives, and is asked again if the service finds a reason to.

docs.title: A confirmation that lands elsewhere
docs.text:
A form in a table row whose question needs a dialog puts the dialog in the spec-form fragment as an out-of-band element, which htmx swaps into the element of the same id wherever it is on the page, beside the form swapped in place. The view's Python does not change, and it sets no header:

<html>
<body>
<h1>Drafts</h1>
{% if not requested_input %}<dialog id="confirm-discard"></dialog>{% endif %}
{% partialdef spec-form inline %}
<form id="discard-drafts" method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {% if not requested_input %}{{ form.non_field_errors }}{% endif %}
  {% for field in form %}{% if not requested_input or field.name not in requested_input.schema %}
    {{ field.errors }}{{ field.label_tag }} {{ field }}
  {% endif %}{% endfor %}
  <button name="save">Discard</button>
</form>
{% if requested_input %}
<dialog id="confirm-discard" hx-swap-oob="true" open>
  <p>{{ requested_input.message }}</p>
  {% for field in requested_input.fields %}
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="{{ field.html_name }}" form="discard-drafts"> {{ field.label }}</label>
  {% endfor %}
  <button name="save" form="discard-drafts">Discard them</button>
</dialog>
{% endif %}
{% endpartialdef %}
</body>
</html>

The URLconf routes it as books/discard-drafts/in-a-dialog/. Every field of the form but the ones asked for is rendered in the form, and the dialog carries the message, the box and a button. They sit outside the form, so each names it with HTML's form attribute, which is what makes them post with it; a control outside the form with no form attribute posts nothing. The page renders the empty dialog only before a question, so whichever way the page is rendered there is one element with its id. An id that matches no element on the page swaps nothing.

docs.title: A confirmation that only posts
docs.text: A button in a list's row posts to a confirmation that never renders a page: set http_method_names = ["post"] with refusal_redirect = True, and as_view() does not look for the shipped template, so the page's templates need not be installed. A refusal goes back to the list as a message. Where messages are unavailable, it answers the refusal's status with an empty body rather than a 500. A page that serves GET or HEAD, or whose refusal is not redirected, is still checked at as_view().

docs.title: Not a gate on an agent route
docs.text: The question is a page's affordance, never a security boundary. On an agent route, the same AdditionalInputRequired goes back to the model as a retry naming the missing argument, and the model can answer confirmed: true itself on its next call, with nobody asked. So nothing that must have a person's yes may rely on this question. For a human gate on an agent route, enable ToolGuard in django-spec-agents, whose approval card a person answers before the tool runs, and keep the spec's tool out of its exempt list.

docs.title: What the request carries
docs.text:
The page reads the request as the JSON views do, with the same attributes and hooks, checked by the same code:

  • route_kwargs says which URL kwargs fill which parameters, a mapping to rename or drop ({"branch": None}) or a tuple of names to allow, as on SpecView. as_view() refuses a bare string and a target or an allowed name the spec does not declare, and two kwargs filling one parameter are refused on the request that captures both.
  • route_refusal_404, on by default on every page, answers a route capture the shape check refuses with Http404, as a URL converter that did not match would: /folders/7/reorder/sideways/, where direction is a choice of up or down, names nothing. The route's arguments are read and checked apart from the post's, after the class-level check and before anything is posted, on GET and POST alike, so the page knows the refused key came from the URL rather than guessing from its name. A refused posted argument is answered as before. route_refusal_404 = False restores the answers of 0.12.0: a route value refused on GET is Django's BadRequest where its type does not parse, and a choice is not checked until the post; on POST it is the page's refusal, with the message prefixed by its name ("direction: Select a valid choice. ..."), or under a confirmation's refusal_redirect that message and a redirect; and the selector page answers 400 with it in errors.
  • get_pool_seeds(request), pool_seeds unless overridden, answers the seeds this request's call is resolved with. It is asked once per request, and every step that resolves a spec callable is handed what it answered: the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, the affordances below, the form's form_kwargs, and dispatch. Seed what the request carries, never the request itself. The class-level check is asked with them too: the page asks has_permission before it reads anything else, through the kernel's authorize, on the seeds the request resolved for its checks, so a check reading a tenant admits the principal on the page as dispatch would.
  • get_server_arguments(request), server_arguments unless overridden, answers the kernel's ServerArguments, and three readers of the call read the server's value for each name it answers for: the page's form, the target's lookup and dispatch. A field of the page's form that the binding binds renders disabled, showing the server's value; one it withholds renders disabled and empty, on GET and on a refused post alike, so the page never shows a value the client posted for it. A disabled field is not read from the post, so a value the client was never offered is never coerced or refused; the binding is laid over the post's arguments before dispatch, and over the route's before the target is found, so a target selector reading a bound parameter finds the row by the server's value. Anything else a template shows - the row's own fields, say - is what it is.

The seeds the spec's checks name are resolved once per request, after the route is read and before the class-level check, by the kernel's resolve_seeds: every registered seed a check names at any of its three questions, as dispatch resolves them. The CallSeeds it returns is handed to the class-level check, the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, and dispatch, so from the class-level check to the service each sees one value of each seed. That holds on the form page, on the formset page, whose scope check dispatch asks on the same seeds, and on the selector page, whose selector reads them. A route the host got wrong is refused before any resolver runs, and a resolver raising PrincipalUnavailable is the host's 403. Since a seed only the object-level or scope check names is resolved ahead of the class-level check too, its resolver runs for a principal that check then refuses, as it does under dispatch, and for every principal, anonymous included. A resolver that reads something only an admitted principal has should raise PrincipalUnavailable for anyone else; any other error it raises reaches the host as a server error, where the class-level check used to answer a 403.

Three steps take no carrier and resolve the seeds again: the form's keywords, where form_kwargs names one; the affordances' pool on a GET and on a post that does not commit, which a target's display, where the page shows one, is presented with too; and, on a post that does not commit under validate_on_refresh, the kernel's bind_arguments. A refused post that presents a display resolves them once more, for the presenter's. So a resolver answering a fresh object answers each of those steps a different one. Write seed resolvers that answer the same each time.

One call context per request. The page creates one plain dict for each request, starting with request, this request, and view, this page, and hands that same object to every kernel call it makes: the class-level check, the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, the affordances, the form's form_kwargs and dispatch. The spec's parameters are read with it too, for the route's check and the post's reading, a validated refresh's included, so a Validator whose parameters declares call_context declares to the page's reading what it declares to dispatch. The kernel's own helpers the page calls around it read the spec with it as well: applying the server's binding checks each bound value against what the spec declares to this request, and a bound value that declaration refuses is the host's ImproperlyConfigured; checking an asked question's keys lets a service ask for a key the spec declares to this request alone. What as_view() checks runs with no request, and reads them with no context: route_kwargs, server_arguments, so a bound name is declared to no call as well, and a list page's paging keys and table order field. So a check, a condition, form_kwargs or the service declaring call_context reads what an earlier stage of the same request put there, and each request gets a dict of its own. The dict is stamped "html" under the kernel's TRANSPORT_KEY, as the JSON views' is, so a callable reading it sees one value in the check, the validator, the service and the presenter, and in the affordances a list page and a form page ask ahead of a post. A selector, a check, a condition, a seed's resolver, form_kwargs or the service naming request or view is handed the one in it, as on the JSON views, and the display's presenter reads the page's seeds as its ambient, never the context.

The checks are the JSON views': as_view() refuses an async def hook, checks server_arguments with the kernel's check_server_arguments against the declared pool_seeds, and refuses a route_kwargs filling a name the binding answers for. On each request, a per-call binding that binds or withholds other names than the declared one, a seed added per call under a bound or withheld name, and a route capture filling a name the server answers for are each refused as ImproperlyConfigured, the last pointing at route_kwargs={name: None}.

BRANCHES = {"main", "harbour"}
CLOSED_BRANCHES = {"harbour"}


class AtABranch(PermissionCheck):
    message = "There is no such branch."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any, *, branch: str) -> bool:
        # branch is a seed, which get_pool_seeds adds.
        return branch in BRANCHES


def branch_open(*, branch: str) -> bool:
    # ``branch`` is a seed, so every transport serving this spec seeds its own.
    return branch not in CLOSED_BRANCHES


stock_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn(), AtABranch()],
    validator=book_validator,
    affordances=[
        Affordance(
            code="branch_closed",
            reason="This branch is closed for stocktaking.",
            when=branch_open,
        ),
    ],
)


class StockBook(SpecFormView):
    spec = stock_book_spec
    template_name = "spec_form_available.html"
    success_url = reverse_lazy("books")
    # The route's branch is a seed, not an argument: drop it.
    route_kwargs = {"branch": None}
    # A book stocked at a branch starts as a draft, whatever the form posts.
    server_arguments = ServerArguments(values={"status": Status.DRAFT})

    def get_pool_seeds(self, request: HttpRequest) -> PoolSeeds:
        # What the request carries, never the request itself.
        return self.pool_seeds.extend(branch=lambda: self.kwargs["branch"])

The URLconf routes it as branches/<branch>/books/new/. Every route under that prefix captures branch, which the spec reads as a seed rather than an argument, so route_kwargs = {"branch": None} drops it from the arguments and every other kwarg is still held strict. AtABranch, a class-level check, names the branch seed, which get_pool_seeds adds and the page asks it with before it offers the form, so a branch it does not know is PermissionDenied on GET and on POST before the form is built. Its status renders disabled with draft selected, and a posted status is dropped: every book it adds is a draft.

docs.title: An operation that is unavailable
docs.text:
A spec's Affordance conditions say whether the operation is possible right now, and the page asks them on GET, after it has found the target, so it never offers a form whose post the spec would refuse at 409:

  • The callable conditions are asked always, through the kernel's unmet_operation_affordance, on a pool seeded_pool builds from the call's own seeds. So a condition reading a seed get_pool_seeds adds, as branch_open above reads branch, is asked with it.
  • When the target is a row and every callable condition is met, the conditions on the row are asked too, as dispatch asks them. A target of None - a create, or a missing row allow_none lets through - is no row, and no row condition is asked about it.
  • The first unmet one is in the context as unavailable: the Affordance itself, whose code and reason a template reads. When every condition is met, unavailable is absent from the context, not None. The fragment renders from the same context, so an hx-get that loads the form carries it too.
  • On a page serving actions, each action's conditions are asked for its own button: unavailable_actions names the unavailable ones, action_buttons answers every one, and unavailable is set only when none is available.

Every callable condition is asked twice on a GET with a row: once alone, then again with the row's conditions, since the kernel's enforce_affordances asks them all as dispatch does. Each seed is resolved twice as well, once for the target's lookup and once for the affordances' pool, and once more for each of the class-level check and the form's form_kwargs that names it. On a page serving actions, every action's conditions are asked so, on GET and again on a refused post's page. Write conditions and seed resolvers that may be asked more than once and answer the same.

The callable conditions are asked first, without a row, so where both kinds are unmet and the row's is declared first, the page names the callable while the post is refused with the row's: dispatch asks in declaration order. The page's answer is advice, and the post's refusal is the authority: the post is dispatched as before, dispatch asks every condition again, and a condition that changed between the two requests is answered by the 409.

A refused post carries the refusal's code in its context, beside the form, for a refusal that has one: ActionUnavailable, whose code is the one the JSON body carries beside its detail. It is absent for every other refusal. The fragment's context carries it too, so a template branches on the stable code rather than on the message.

There is no default template yet, so a host's template says it:

{% if unavailable %}<p class="unavailable" data-code="{{ unavailable.code }}">{{ unavailable.reason }}</p>{% endif %}
<form method="post">{% csrf_token %}
  {% if code == "branch_closed" %}<p class="next"><a href="/branches/">Choose another branch.</a></p>{% endif %}
  <fieldset{% if unavailable %} disabled{% endif %}>{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button></fieldset>
</form>

On the closed branch above, the page says why and disables the form, and a post made anyway comes back at 409 with the reason among the form's errors and the link to another branch beside it.

docs.title: An htmx request
docs.text:
Turning htmx on is a template change. The view answers every request with the page unless htmx asked for less, and then answers the same outcome with the part of the page the request swaps, rendered from the same template. Wrap the page's form in {% partialdef spec-form inline %}, give the form hx-post and a target, and, for a success answered in place, define spec-result:

<html>
<body>
<h1>New book</h1>
{% partialdef spec-form inline %}
<form method="post" hx-post="{% url 'add-book' %}" hx-swap="outerHTML">
  {% csrf_token %}{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button>
</form>
{% endpartialdef %}
{% partialdef spec-result %}
<p id="saved">Added {{ result.value.title }}.</p>
{% endpartialdef %}
</body>
</html>

urlpatterns = [
    # The same view as a plain page: only the template changed.
    path(
        "books/new/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=add_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_form_htmx.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
        ),
        name="add-book",
    ),
    path("books/", books, name="books"),
]

The view's Python does not change: inline renders the form where it stands on the page, and the same block is addressable on its own as spec_form_htmx.html#spec-form, which is where the view looks for it by default. The tag and that #name address are Django 6.0's. Below 6.0, install django-template-partials (23.3 or later, the first with partialdef) and configure it in TEMPLATES: its tag as a builtin, and its loader around the project's own.

# settings.py, below Django 6.0 only: from 6.0 Django has the tag and the
# address itself, and this would register a second partialdef over its own.
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "OPTIONS": {
            # The tag as a builtin, so the page's template needs no
            # {% load partials %}, which Django 6.0 would not find.
            "builtins": ["template_partials.templatetags.partials"],
            # Its loader around the project's own, for the page.html#name
            # address. Adding "template_partials" to INSTALLED_APPS sets this
            # one up for you, and the builtin above still has to be named.
            "loaders": [
                (
                    "template_partials.loader.Loader",
                    [
                        "django.template.loaders.filesystem.Loader",
                        "django.template.loaders.app_directories.Loader",
                    ],
                )
            ],
        },
    }
]

The builtin is the part that is easy to miss. Adding "template_partials" to INSTALLED_APPS sets up the loader and nothing else, so the page's template fails to parse at {% partialdef %}; and a {% load partials %} in the template instead would break it again on Django 6.0, which has the tag itself and no such library. From 6.0, configure none of this. Without either, the address is a TemplateDoesNotExist. A fragment kept in a file of its own, or under another name, is one attribute, fragment_template_name, and renders on any Django. That is how the shipped page carries its form: an htmx request to a page naming no template is answered with django_spec_html/spec_form_fragment.html, with nothing to configure on any Django.

Choosing the fragment by the request's target. One URL can answer htmx requests aimed at different elements with different parts of the page, such as a dialog and a panel. Override get_fragment_template_names() and read the HX-Target header off self.request; return the shipped answer for every target the override does not name:

class AddBookByTarget(SpecFormView):
    spec = add_book_spec
    success_url = reverse_lazy("books")

    def get_fragment_template_names(self) -> list[str]:
        if self.request.headers.get("HX-Target") == "dialog":
            return ["spec_form_dialog_fragment.html"]
        return super().get_fragment_template_names()

A request for the target dialog renders spec_form_dialog_fragment.html; any other htmx request renders the form fragment the view would have, and a request without htmx is the page, since the method is read only for a fragment. The override picks a template and nothing else, so the outcome is the same in every target.

Multi-step flows are out of scope for the pages. A wizard, or a payment that is started and then polled, is a sequence of requests whose state the page does not carry: the view holds nothing between one post and the next. Serve each step as a page of its own, one URL and one spec per step, and keep what the steps share in the service, such as a draft row or an order whose status each step reads and moves. The next step's page then finds its state from its route, as any page finds its target, and a step reached out of order is the spec's own refusal.

Which requests get the fragment. A request whose HX-Request header is true, unless it is boosted (HX-Boosted) or a history restore (HX-History-Restore-Request): a boosted link or form swaps the whole body, and a history restore after a cache miss needs the whole page back, so both get the page. The view reads django-htmx's request.htmx where its middleware set it and the three headers where it did not, so a project with django-htmx and one without get the same answer; it imports nothing from django-htmx. The rule is one method, wants_fragment(request), to override. Every answer sets Vary on those three headers, the page's included, since one URL answers two bodies and a cache keyed on fewer would hand a fragment to a page load.

What the fragment answers, outcome by outcome:

  • GET renders the form fragment, unbound, so an hx-get can load the form into a dialog.
  • A refusal the page re-renders is the form fragment, bound the same way and from the same context, at 200 where the page answers 4xx: htmx swaps no 4xx response by default, so a refusal answered at one would land nowhere. The table above has each row, and the outcome stays in the body and in the map.
  • A success is fragment_success(result). Where the fragment template defines spec-result, that is rendered in place at 200, and HX-Trigger: spec-succeeded names an event for the rest of the page to listen for. Its context is result, view, spec and extra_context, and no form, since the post's form is done with. Otherwise it is HX-Redirect to a safe next when the page reads one, else to get_success_url(result), at 200 and never a 302: an XHR follows a 302 itself and would swap the next page into the form. The URL is encoded and checked as the page's redirect is, so a path outside ASCII arrives as the page's Location would, and an unsafe scheme such as javascript: raises DisallowedRedirect in both modes. The answer passes back through the host's middleware like any other, so a cookie set for the request, such as the session a sign-in rotates, is set on it. Override the method for HX-Location.
  • A denial is raised in both modes alike, for the host's handlers.

The event a success triggers is the page's to name. Three attributes, on every page with a post, shape the success answered in place:

Attribute Default Sends success_trigger "spec-succeeded" an event's name as it is; a mapping of event names to payloads as the JSON htmx reads, each payload the event's detail; None sends no trigger success_trigger_timing "receive" the trigger in HX-Trigger; "swap" in HX-Trigger-After-Swap, "settle" in HX-Trigger-After-Settle success_refresh False HX-Refresh: true and an empty body in place of the result fragment, which the page then need not define, with the trigger beside it

get_success_trigger(result) returns success_trigger; override it for a payload that depends on the result:

class NewNote(SpecFormView):
    success_trigger_timing = "settle"

    def get_success_trigger(self, result):
        return {"note-saved": {"id": result.value.pk}}

A payload is encoded with Django's DjangoJSONEncoder, so a date, a Decimal or a UUID arrives as a string, and with every character outside ASCII escaped, so the header carries it whole. as_view() refuses an empty name, a mapping with no names or a key that is not one, a timing that is not one of the three, and a success_refresh that is not a bool. Whether a payload encodes is known only when it is sent, so one that does not raises ImproperlyConfigured then. A refresh with a trigger timed to "swap" or "settle" is refused at as_view(): htmx fires HX-Trigger and then reloads, so a trigger waiting for a swap never fires. None of these reaches a post without htmx, which is redirected as before, nor an HX-Redirect.

A template with no fragment at the address answers htmx with Django's TemplateDoesNotExist naming it - spec_form.html#spec-form, or the fragment_template_name that is missing - and never with the page instead, which swapped into a form's target would nest a second layout inside it.

No htmx header reaches the spec. The mode is read only after the outcome is decided, to choose the wrapper: the arguments are the form's fields and the route's kwargs, and dispatch is called the same way in both modes. So a spec cannot branch on the mode, and its outcome on the page and in a fragment is one outcome. One header is read before dispatch, HX-Trigger-Name, and only to stop a post committing on a page that names its commit button and, on a post that does not commit, to say which errors a validated refresh shows.

A denial is the host's to answer, for htmx too. The view raises PermissionDenied and Http404 in both modes, on every page, and a list row's or a confirmation's denial is answered by the same two handlers. A handler answering an htmx request with a bare 403 or 404 shows nothing, since htmx swaps no 4xx. htmx acts on HX-Redirect and HX-Refresh whatever the status, so a handler can keep the status and still send the visitor somewhere:

def handler403(request: HttpRequest, exception: Exception | None = None) -> HttpResponse:
    if request.headers.get("HX-Request") != "true":
        if request.user.is_authenticated:
            response = permission_denied(request, exception)
        else:
            response = redirect_to_login(request.get_full_path())
    else:
        response = HttpResponse(status=403)
        if request.user.is_authenticated:
            response["HX-Refresh"] = "true"
        else:
            here = request.headers.get("HX-Current-URL", request.get_full_path())
            response["HX-Redirect"] = redirect_to_login(here).url
    patch_vary_headers(response, ("HX-Request",))
    return response


def handler404(request: HttpRequest, exception: Exception | None = None) -> HttpResponse:
    """The host's 404: Django's page for a browser, and for htmx a refresh."""
    if request.headers.get("HX-Request") != "true":
        response = page_not_found(request, exception)
    else:
        response = HttpResponse(status=404)
        response["HX-Refresh"] = "true"
    patch_vary_headers(response, ("HX-Request",))
    return response

Defined in the root URLconf as handler403 and handler404, they answer as follows:

Without htmx With htmx handler403, anonymous a redirect to the login page, back to the page asked for HX-Redirect to the login page, back to the page the request came from handler403, signed in Django's 403 page HX-Refresh handler404 Django's 404 page HX-Refresh

The reload answers with the 403 page only where the page itself refuses on GET: the spec's class-level check, or the object-level check on the row the route names. A denial only the operation raises, from inside the service, does not recur on GET, so the reload shows the form again, empty, and what was typed is gone; a host whose services refuse that way answers those in the form instead, by raising a ServiceError. An htmx action on a list row that went away since the page was drawn is a 404, and the reload shows the list without it; a page whose own route names the vanished row reloads to the 404 page. HX-Refresh on a request fired by a load or a polling every trigger that keeps failing reloads the page over and over, so such a request should target a URL that does not answer 403 or 404. The view's Vary never reaches a denial, which is raised rather than answered, so each handler sets its own on HX-Request, since it answers the two kinds of request differently.

docs.title: Adding a formset row over htmx
docs.text: The formset page's shipped add button posts into the rows and appends the one form it is answered with, beside an out-of-band TOTAL_FORMS; a post at the list's maximum is a 204. Adding a row has what chooses that answer and how a project's own template takes it.

docs.title: Editing an existing set
docs.text: The formset page renders a Validator's formset_class as it is declared. A model formset there edits the spec's collection_selector_spec: one prefilled form a row, a deleted row sent whole with DELETE true, a row left out left alone. Editing a set has the example and what a post sends.

docs.title: A formset over any Validator
docs.text:
A many spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator gets a formset page by naming its row form, form_class, as the form page does:

SpecFormSetView.as_view(spec=add_books_spec, form_class=BookForm, success_url="/books/")

The page builds one formset_factory of it, within the spec's many_min_length and many_max_length, every form built with get_form_kwargs(). Each form renders and is read, and is never validated: a row's refusal lands on the form that sent it, and a refusal of the whole set is the formset's non-form errors. The rule over the set is the Validator's own validated_many, which raises it under non_field_errors; the page adds none. as_view() checks the row form against each row's parameters, not the call's top level, with the form page's checks; a route and server_arguments fill the top level only, so a required row parameter the form leaves out passes only where the server's own keys fill it.

A spec with a collection_selector_spec edits its set. GET builds one prefilled form a row of the set the selector resolves, each carrying the row's key in a hidden field named for the model's primary key, then the extra forms; INITIAL_FORMS is the set's count. A post sends each initial form's row with its key, a deleted one whole with DELETE true, and leaves a row it does not post alone; an extra form ticked for deletion sends nothing. The rows declare the key, optional so a new row sends none, and a boolean DELETE where rows may be deleted, which offers the box:

@dataclasses.dataclass
class EditedNote:
    title: str
    id: int | None = None
    DELETE: bool = False

A key missing from an initial form, or naming a row outside the set, refuses that row on its form; the page reads the key and validates nothing else. Rows declaring no key are refused when the set is first built, and a DELETE that is not a boolean at as_view().

docs.title: Coming from Django's FormView
docs.text: A refused post answers 400 here where Django's FormView answers 200: the status is the kernel's refusal status, the refusals table has each row. A host moving a form onto a page of this package updates its tests that assert 200 on an invalid post. A post through htmx is unchanged, since the fragment answers a refusal at 200.

docs.title: Under ASGI
docs.text: The pages are sync views and serve under ASGI. Django runs a sync view on a thread there, so a project on an ASGI server needs nothing of the page. There is no async page: Django renders a template response on a thread already, but the page's own database work before it renders, which is admission and the spec's checks, dispatch, the target's lookup and the list's COUNT, would raise SynchronousOnlyOperation on the event loop. An async page would have to wrap every one of those in a thread hop, which is the hop Django already makes for a sync view. AsyncSpecView differs because it answers JSON presented inside adispatch, with no template to render and nothing else of the page to carry.

docs.title: One form, several operations
docs.text:
A form whose buttons run different operations - save a draft, publish it, delete it - is one page. actions maps each submit button's name to the spec it runs, and replaces spec:

(
    path(
        "posts/<int:pk>/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            actions={"save": save_post_spec, "publish": publish_post_spec},
            route_kwargs=("pk",),
            success_url=reverse_lazy("posts"),
        ),
    ),
)
  • A committing post runs the action whose button it carries: the one key of actions in request.POST, whatever its value, so a <button name="publish"> with no value names publish. A post naming none, or more than one, is Django's BadRequest, a 400, and nothing runs. The chosen spec is the one the post is admitted, finds its target, is validated and dispatched by, and the one a refused post's page is rendered with.
  • GET renders the first action's spec: the page, its admission, its target and its form are the first action's.
  • Each action's button answers its own availability. GET asks every action's affordances, each of the target the first action found, so a condition on the row is asked of the row the page shows. The context carries unavailable_actions, each unavailable action's key mapped to its first unmet Affordance, absent when every action is available, and action_buttons, every action's key beside that Affordance or None, in the order actions lists them. unavailable is set only when no action is available: the first action's Affordance. So a titled note's "Publish" can be unavailable while its "Save" is not, and only "Publish" is refused. A post naming an unavailable action is refused at 409 by that action's own dispatch, as on a page with one spec.
  • An action the user may not run is disabled, and says nothing. GET asks every action after the first the checks its post would run before dispatch: its admission and class-level permissions, then its object check on the row the page shows (its scope check on a set, or on none), and, with route_refusal_404 on, the default, a route capture its own parameters refuse; with it off the capture is left to its post, as it is for the first action. The context carries refused_actions, the frozenset of the refused keys, absent when none is. A refused action's affordances are not asked: it is in neither unavailable_actions nor unavailable, and its action_buttons entry is None, so nothing says why. The first action's refusal is still the page's own 403 or 404, and a post naming a refused action is refused as it always was, 403 or 404, before anything runs. So a reader's page shows "Publish" disabled where only an editor may publish. When the first action is unavailable and every other is refused, unavailable is not set: every button is disabled and the form's fields are not.
  • A refused post's page keeps each action's state. A refused post's page, and its fragment under htmx, renders unavailable_actions, refused_actions, action_buttons and unavailable as a GET of the page would, asked of the target that post found: the action that ran stands where GET's first does, and every other action, the first included, is asked as above. So a "Save" refused for a blank title leaves "Publish" disabled beside its reason, and a post naming the unavailable "Publish" answers 409 with its button disabled, its reason beside it as well as in the refusal's own error. With route_refusal_404 off, a post whose route the target's reads refuse found no target, and one whose route another action's reads refuse is asked of none of them; either page carries none of the four. A page with one spec re-renders a refused post as it always did, with no unavailable.
  • The success is page-wide. success_url and success_message serve every action. get_success_url(result) and get_success_message(result) read which one ran as self.action_name, the key, set before the post is dispatched; it is None on GET and on a page without actions.
  • The shipped templates render one submit button per action, named by its key and labelled with it capitalised, in the order actions lists them, in place of the one button. A refused action's button is disabled with nothing beside it. An unavailable action's button is disabled and its reason shown, in a paragraph carrying its key as data-action and its code as data-code; the others stay usable, and the form's fields are disabled only when no action is available. They loop over action_buttons rather than unavailable_actions.items, which an action keyed items would shadow. A project's own template renders its own.

SpecConfirmView takes actions the same way, every action a spec with no Validator: a confirmation's "Archive" and "Delete" buttons are one page.

as_view() checks every action as it checks a page's spec - its Validator, its parameters against the route, the binding, the seeds and a confirmation's posted_arguments - each refusal naming the action, as in SpecFormView.actions['publish']. It also refuses actions beside spec, an empty mapping, a key that is not a non-empty string, a redirect_field_name that is an action's key, any commit_button beside actions (an actions page commits only through an action's button, and a post naming none answers 400), on a confirmation an action keyed like a posted_arguments name or csrfmiddlewaretoken, which every post carries, and actions on a page that takes none, such as SpecFormSetView. On SpecFormView every action is validated by a FormValidator of one form class, or shares the page's form_class, since the page posts one form, and no key is the name of one of its fields, which every submit posts.

docs.title: A post that does not commit
docs.text:
A form that refreshes a dependent choice, adds a row or searches posts without meaning to run the operation. commit_button names the submit button whose post commits, and every other post re-renders the form. It is None by default, and then every post commits, as a page that does not set it always has.

class AddEditionForm(forms.Form):
    # Choosing an author posts the form again, through htmx where it is
    # loaded, so the books offered below are theirs.
    author = forms.ModelChoiceField(
        queryset=Author.objects.all(),
        widget=forms.Select(
            attrs={
                "hx-post": "",
                "hx-trigger": "change",
                "hx-target": "closest form",
                "hx-swap": "outerHTML",
            }
        ),
    )
    book = forms.ModelChoiceField(queryset=Book.objects.none())
    number = forms.IntegerField(min_value=1)

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        # The books of the author the post names, and none until it names one.
        author = self.data.get(self.add_prefix("author"))
        if str(author).isdigit():
            self.fields["book"].queryset = Book.objects.filter(author_id=author)


def add_edition(*, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Edition:
    return Edition.objects.create(book=data["book"], number=data["number"])


add_edition_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_edition,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(AddEditionForm),
)

The form narrows its book choices by the author the post names, and offers none until it names one. It reads the author from self.data, which holds the string the page's post carried; in the form the Validator binds, the author is the coerced number itself, so the same __init__ serves both.

The URLconf routes it as editions/new/, with commit_button="add", and its form is a file of its own, so it renders on any Django:

<form method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">{% csrf_token %}
  {{ form }}
  <button name="add">Add the edition</button>
  <button name="refresh" formnovalidate>Show their books</button>
</form>

Choosing an author posts the form, through htmx where it is loaded, and "Show their books" does the same without it. Neither carries add, so neither runs the operation; the form comes back with the books of the author posted, and "Add the edition" commits. A book by another author is refused on that post, since the Validator's form is narrowed by the same post.

Which posts commit, decided by one method, commits(request), to override for another rule, such as two buttons that both commit:

  • The post's data must carry the button's name. A browser posts the name and value of the submit button that was pressed and of no other, with or without JavaScript. htmx does the same for a form it submits, and posts no button's name for a request a control issues itself, such as the author picker's hx-post.
  • Under htmx 2, HX-Trigger-Name can stop a commit, never make one. It names the element the request came from: the form, whose name is never posted, or a control, whose own value always is. A header naming a key the post carries, other than the button, is another control's request, and does not commit even where the button's name reached the data some other way, such as an inherited hx-vals. A form's own name, or no header at all, leaves the decision to the data, which is what decides for every client: a browser and htmx alike post the pressed button's name.
  • Enter presses the first submit button in the form, so put the commit button first, as the template above does; a refresh button placed before it would turn Enter into a refresh. Give a refresh button formnovalidate, so the browser posts the form with its required fields still blank.

What a post that does not commit renders is the page GET renders, with the form bound to the post:

  • It is admitted and finds its target as GET does, so a principal the spec refuses is refused, and the context carries target, the count of a set, target_display and unavailable as GET's does.
  • The form is built through form_kwargs like every other form the page builds, bound to the post, so a choice its constructor narrows - by a keyword, or by a value posted - is narrowed again.
  • Nothing is dispatched and nothing validated: the form shows the values posted and no error, and a required field left blank is not called required. asked_fields are held back, as on GET, unless the refusal names one, under validate_on_refresh below.
  • The context carries refreshed, True, for a template that needs to tell; it is absent from every other render.
  • The page answers 200, and an htmx request the form's fragment at 200.

commit_button is checked at as_view(): None, or a non-empty string that names no field of the form, since a field is posted by every submit and could not say which one commits.

docs.title: Validating a post that does not commit
docs.text:
A field checked as a person leaves it, rather than when the form is sent: validate_on_refresh shows, on a post that does not commit, what its commit would refuse. It is False by default, and the form then shows no error, as above. It has no effect without a commit_button, since every post then commits.

class CheckedEditionForm(AddEditionForm):
    # Leaving the number posts the form, so a taken number is refused as typed.
    number = forms.IntegerField(
        min_value=1,
        widget=forms.NumberInput(
            attrs={
                "hx-post": "",
                "hx-trigger": "change",
                "hx-target": "closest form",
                "hx-swap": "outerHTML",
            }
        ),
    )
    # The form's own, and no column of the edition's.
    copies = forms.IntegerField(min_value=1, required=False)

    def clean(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        cleaned = super().clean() or {}
        book, number = cleaned.get("book"), cleaned.get("number")
        if book and number and Edition.objects.filter(book=book, number=number).exists():
            self.add_error("number", f"{book.title} already has edition {number}.")
        return cleaned


check_edition_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_edition,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(CheckedEditionForm),
)

The URLconf routes it as editions/new/checked/, with commit_button="add" and validate_on_refresh=True, on the same templates as editions/new/. Leaving the number posts the form, and a number the book already has is refused there; choosing an author calls nothing else required; "Show their books" shows every error the form has.

  • The post is bound as its commit would bind it, through the kernel's bind_arguments: the form's values and the route's kwargs read as a commit reads them, the server's binding laid over them, under the page's unknown_arguments, with the principal admitted, the target the page found, the request's seeds and its call context. So a form_kwargs naming a seed is handed it, and an update's own unique value is not taken by its own row.
  • Nothing is dispatched and no success_message is sent. The page answers 200, and an htmx request the form's fragment at 200, with refreshed in the context as on any post that does not commit.
  • The refusal is placed on the form as a refused commit's is, by add_argument_errors, beside the page's own form validated. While a field fails the shape check - a required field blank, a number that does not parse - the kernel never runs the Validator, but the page's form, built as the Validator's is, still answers for the rest: a field's clean_<field>(), a length, the form's clean(). So a refresh shows every error its commit would refuse in one post, not the shape's first and the form's after it. On editions/new/checked/, "Show their books" with copies that do not parse and a number the book already has shows both: the copies' error is the shape check's, the number's is the form's clean(). A partial page's form is not validated beside the refusal, since validated whole it would call every blank field required.
  • HX-Trigger-Name decides which errors.
