Where it names one of the form's fields, as the field posts it - its html_name - only that field's errors are shown, the shape check's and the form's own alike, and no non-field error: a person has not reached the rest of the form yet. Every other refresh - no header, the form's own name, a refresh button, one part of a multi-widget field such as when_0 - shows every error, the refusal's and the form's own.
  • No provider runs. bind_arguments runs neither the spec's input_data nor a kwargs provider, and that is the one difference in how the post is bound. A field input_data fills is judged as posted: a required one left blank is refused by the refresh, and accepted by the commit, which the provider fills. What the service, an unmet affordance or a conflict refuses is the commit's alone, since nothing is dispatched.

docs.title: Returning where the page was opened from
docs.text:
A page linked to from the third page of a list should save and go back to the third page, not to the first one, which is where success_url points. redirect_field_name names the key that carries that URL, as Django's LoginView names next. The edit page in the URLconf above sets it:

SpecFormView.as_view(
    spec=edit_book_spec,
    success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
    redirect_field_name="next",
)

The list links to the page as /books/7/edit/?next=/books/%3Fpage%3D3, and a save redirects to /books/?page=3.

  • None, the default, reads nothing, as Django's own FormView reads nothing. Every page follows the URL it was posted with only when its view says so, so a page that never names the key never redirects anywhere a client chose.
  • Once named, the value is read as LoginView reads it: from the post, then from the query. A value posted empty therefore masks the query's.
  • It is used only where it is safe: Django's url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme must allow it against the request's own host, with https required on a secure request. Another host (https://evil.example/), a scheme-relative URL (//evil.example) and an http:// URL posted over https are ignored, and the success goes to get_success_url(result) as it would without the key. So the page is not an open redirect.
  • It wins over get_success_url(result), an override included. Under htmx the HX-Redirect goes to the same URL, but a spec-result fragment is still rendered in place: it answers where the form was and navigates nowhere, and its context carries next for a link back.
  • It never reaches dispatch. The page's arguments are its form's fields and its route, so a key the form does not declare is never read as one, and the closed argument set has nothing to refuse.
  • It survives a refused post. The context carries redirect_field_name and next, the safe URL, under those two fixed names rather than under the key's own as LoginView puts it, so a key such as errors cannot overwrite what the page renders. The shipped templates post them back as a hidden input, and post to the page's own URL, so a next in the query is kept too. A template of the project's own adds the input itself:
{% if next %}<input type="hidden" name="{{ redirect_field_name }}" value="{{ next }}">{% endif %}

Neither key is in the context where there is no safe URL, so an unsafe value is never written back into the page. get_redirect_url() answers the safe value, or "": a fragment_success of a host's own reads it as self.get_redirect_url() or self.get_success_url(result).

as_view() refuses a redirect_field_name that is not a non-empty string, that names a field of the form, whose value would be read as the URL, and one that is the commit_button, whose value would be read the same way. The formset page and the confirmation page read it as this page does, and the confirmation page can also send a refusal back.

docs.title: A success message
docs.text:
success_message is sent through django.contrib.messages on every success: the page's redirect, the HX-Redirect and the result fragment alike. It is formatted as Django's SuccessMessageMixin formats its own, % with the form's cleaned data, so "Edition %(number)s added." above reads the number posted, as the form cleaned it. The cleaned data is the result's data, what the Validator's form handed the service; on a partial page a field left blank is not in it.

get_success_message(result) answers it, to override for a message that reads what the operation returned:

class AddBookThenSayWhich(SpecFormView):
    def get_success_message(self, result: DispatchResult) -> str:
        return f"Book {result.value.pk} added."
  • Without the messages middleware it is skipped, and never raises Django's MessageFailure: a message needs the store the middleware puts on the request, which the app installed alone does not, and the write has already committed.
  • A refusal, a confirmation page and a post that does not commit send none. The message is sent once the operation has run.
  • An empty message, the default, sends nothing.

docs.title: A spec that answers a file
docs.text:
A spec whose presenter is the kernel's FilePresenter answers its success with the file, not a redirect: an export, a report, a signed PDF. The page builds the response as the selector page builds a file's, a FileResponse, or a StreamingHttpResponse for an iterable of bytes, with Content-Disposition: attachment naming the file. as_attachment = False answers inline, for a browser to show a PDF in place.

export_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=export_minutes,
    permissions=(IsAuthenticated,),
    validator=FormValidator(ExportForm),
    presenter=FilePresenter("text/csv", filename="minutes.csv", render=as_csv),
)

path("minutes/export/", SpecFormView.as_view(spec=export_spec, success_url="/minutes/"))
  • No success message and no redirect. The file is the answer, so success_message, success_url and the way back are not read on a success. A refusal is answered as on any page.
  • A None result is answered as any success, the redirect and the message, for a spec the kernel lets answer nothing (allow_none).
  • The shipped form is posted natively. The context carries presents_file where the spec, or any of the page's actions, presents a file, and the shipped form and confirmation render hx-boost="false" for it, so a base.html that boosts the page does not turn the post into an htmx request, which cannot save a download. A template of the project's own reads the same key; under htmx the file is answered all the same, with no HX-Redirect and no trigger.
  • as_view() refuses a file spec the kernel's file_output refuses, such as one declared many: a list of files has no answer.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Everything below is exported from django_spec_html directly, and from the subpackage it is listed under. Import from the package root in application code; the subpackage paths are where each name is defined. Kernel names these views read - ServiceSpec, dispatch, the refusals - are documented on the kernel's site.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
This package defines none. The argument reader reads one of the kernel's:

  • SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH: the longest list an array parameter with no max_length of its own takes. It is the kernel's key, read by the kernel, and keeps its name here. See how long a list may be.

docs.title: SpecFormView
docs.text:
Bases: SpecPageBase

A ServiceSpec validated by a form, served as the page a person fills that form in on.

The spec's Validator must be a FormValidator, and its form class is the page's form:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/new/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(spec=add_book_spec, success_url=reverse_lazy("books")),
    ),
]

GET renders template_name with an unbound form under form, beside view and spec: the names Django's FormView uses, with extra_context merged in as Django's ContextMixin does. The spec's class-level permission check runs first, through authorize, so a page is never offered to a principal the post would refuse.

The page's template is optional. template_name is django_spec_html/spec_form.html by default, a template this package ships: a plain document with no stylesheet, script or htmx attribute, holding the target pane, an unmet affordance's reason with the form disabled, and the form - its errors, a question's message and the field it asks for, and a submit button posting commit_button's name where one is set - inside a POST form with its token. It is found as any app's templates are, so a project lists django_spec_html in INSTALLED_APPS with APP_DIRS on, and as_view() refuses a page rendering it that no template engine finds. Its form is a file of its own, django_spec_html/spec_form_fragment.html, which the page includes and an htmx request is answered with, on every Django. Override either file the Django way, with one of the same name in a template directory found first, or django_spec_html/base.html, the document every shipped page extends; or set template_name to a page of the project's own.

An update's page shows the row it updates. Every GET then finds its target as dispatch would, through resolve_target on the route's kwargs, coerced as a post's are: the row or set a target selector resolves, or None for a create. A check refusing it - the object-level check on a row, the scope check on a set or on None - raises PermissionDenied, as the post would be refused; a missing row or a selector's ServiceNotFound raises Http404; and a route value the spec's parameters refuse raises Http404 too, or Django's BadRequest with route_refusal_404 off. The form shows a row's values for its own fields: a ModelForm of the row's model is built on a copy of it, as the Validator binds one, and any other form takes the row's values for the enabled fields it names as its initial. So a file the row holds is shown, with the clear checkbox an optional file's ClearableFileInput offers beside it. A create, a collection target and a missing row allow_none lets through show an empty form.

POST starts as GET does: the route first, then that check, and only then is the form built from the post. A refused post is answered with the page again, and dispatch's shape check comes before its own permission check, so without it a principal the spec refuses would be shown the page - every row a choice field lists, and extra_context - by posting a malformed form, and a form whose constructor reads rows would read them for that principal. The Grant it returns goes to dispatch, so the class-level check runs once.

Then the post finds its target, as GET does, before the form is built or read, so the form a refused post re-renders is built on the row as the page's was, its held file and clear checkbox shown. The target answers before the shape check: the object-level and scope checks and a missing row refuse a malformed post as they would a well-formed one, rather than dispatch re-rendering the page for a principal the row refuses. Dispatch is handed the target and the grant resolve_target returns, so it looks nothing up again and asks no check twice. A route value the target's reads refuse is a 404 before the post is read; with route_refusal_404 off it is left to dispatch, whose one refusal carries it beside the form's own.

POST binds the form to the post and reads the arguments through its own widgets - a checkbox is True or False, a multi-select a list - because that is how Django reads a form, and a flat reading refuses a checkbox's "on". Only the form's fields are read, so the CSRF token and a named submit button never become arguments, and a disabled field is not read at all, as the form ignores what is posted for it. A field left blank is absent, as it is to the form. A number, date or date-time the field reads in one of its input formats - 10/25/2006, a localized 12,50 - is sent on in the form the shape check reads, through the field's own to_python, so the shape check never refuses what the form accepts. The URL kwargs are merged last, so the route wins a clash, as in request_arguments. Each is an argument, so the spec declares each one: a kwarg it does not is the host's misconfiguration, raised as ImproperlyConfigured under either unknown_arguments policy rather than answered as a refused post. Then dispatch:

  • A success redirects to get_success_url(result): success_url through Django's resolve_url by default, so a reverse_lazy or a URL name works, and a subclass overrides it to read the result. A view naming redirect_field_name - "next", as Django's LoginView names it - redirects instead to the URL the post or its query carries under that key, where get_redirect_url() finds it safe, so a page linked to from a list returns to the list.
  • A refusal of the arguments - InvalidArguments, or a ServiceValidationError - re-renders the bound form at 400 with the refusal placed on it by add_argument_errors. A service's string or list detail is about the whole form.
  • Any other refusal re-renders it with the message as a non-field error: ServiceConflict at 409, any other ServiceError at 422, UnsupportedMediaType at 415, any other DispatchError at 400. The statuses are error_response's, read from the one map, so a client reading a refused post - Turbo, which will not render a failed post answered 200 - reads it the same way.
  • A question, AdditionalInputRequired, re-renders it at 422, the message as a non-field error, as the confirmation page below.
  • NotPermitted and PrincipalUnavailable raise Django's PermissionDenied, and a not-found result or ServiceNotFound raises Http404, for the host's own 403 and 404 pages.

The confirmation page is an AdditionalInputRequired rendered. Its schema is checked first by the kernel's check_requested_input, with the call's seeds, so a question no route could hear answered - a key no parameter declares, one a seed fills, a shape a transport cannot render, a type the parameter refuses - raises ImproperlyConfigured on the page and in the fragment alike, and is never rendered. Then the bound form is re-rendered with every value posted, and the context carries requested_input: the message, the schema, and the fields, the form's bound fields the schema names. The page builds no widget from a schema. The answer is a field the spec's form declares, an optional BooleanField whose absent box cleans to False, and asked_fields holds it back until a question names it: it is taken out of the form each GET and every other refusal renders, so it posts nothing of its own, and shown empty when asked, so a yes is never carried over to a question asked again. A key no field declares is asked by the message alone. The target is found and a set counted again for the post that asked, so the page says what it found then.

Two wrappers, one outcome. The view decides what a request ends in once - a success, or the refusal's Outcome - and only then reads who asked, to choose how to answer it. Every request gets the page above unless wants_fragment says htmx asked for less, and then the same outcome is answered as a fragment, at the same URL:

  • The form renders get_fragment_template_names() where the page renders template_name, from the same context: on GET, and on every refusal the page re-renders, at 200 rather than the page's 4xx, since htmx swaps no 4xx by default. A shipped page's is its fragment file. For a page of the project's own the default address is <template_name>#spec-form, a {% partialdef %} inside the page's own template, which Django 6.0 resolves; below it, django-template-partials does, with its tag named in TEMPLATES as a builtin ("builtins": ["template_partials.templatetags.partials"]) and its loader around the project's. A template with no fragment at the address is Django's TemplateDoesNotExist naming it, never the page, which swapped into a form's target would nest a second layout inside it.
  • A success is fragment_success(result): HX-Redirect to get_redirect_url() or get_success_url(result), or the spec-result fragment in place.
  • A denial is raised in both modes alike, for the host's handlers.

Both wrappers set Vary on the three headers the choice reads. No htmx header reaches dispatch: the arguments are the form's fields and the route's kwargs whichever wrapper answers, so a spec cannot tell the two apart. One header is read before dispatch, HX-Trigger-Name, and only to stop a post committing and, on a post that does not commit, to say which errors a refresh validated under validate_on_refresh shows, both below.

A post that does not commit. A form that refreshes a dependent choice, adds a row or searches posts without meaning to run the operation. commit_button names the submit button whose post commits; None, the default, commits every post. Once set, commits(request) decides: a post whose data does not carry that name, or an htmx request whose HX-Trigger-Name names another control the post carries, is the page GET renders, admitted and with its target, its affordances and asked_fields held back as GET's are, but with the form bound to the post and built through form_kwargs as every form is, so a choice its constructor narrows by a posted value is narrowed again. Nothing is dispatched and nothing validated: the form shows no error, and the context carries refreshed, absent from every other render. It answers 200 on the page, and the form's fragment at 200 under htmx.

Validating a post that does not commit. validate_on_refresh shows on such a post what its commit would refuse, so a field is checked as a person leaves it. The post is read as a commit reads it, the binding laid over it, and bound through the kernel's bind_arguments with the principal, the target the page found, the request's seeds and its call context: the shape check and the Validator, and nothing dispatched, no success_message sent. Its refusal is placed on the form as a refused commit's is, beside the page's own form validated on a whole call, so a field the shape check refuses does not hide what the form's own checks - clean_<field>(), a length, clean() - say of the rest, at 200 still, with refreshed in the context. Where HX-Trigger-Name names one of the form's fields, as its html_name, the name it posts under, only that field's errors are shown, the shape check's and the form's own alike, and no non-field error; on every other refresh, every error. It runs no provider, as bind_arguments runs neither input_data nor kwargs: a field the spec's input_data fills is judged as posted, so a required one left blank is refused by the refresh and accepted by the commit, which the provider fills.

A success message. success_message, where it is set, is sent through django.contrib.messages on every success - the redirect, the HX-Redirect and the result fragment alike - formatted by get_success_message(result), % with the Validator's data, the form's cleaned data here, as Django's SuccessMessageMixin formats it. Without the messages middleware it is skipped, and never raises MessageFailure. A refusal, a confirmation page and a post that does not commit send none.

A spec presenting a file, through the kernel's FilePresenter, answers its success with the file, built as SpecSelectorView builds one: no redirect, no HX-Redirect and no success message. A None result is answered as any success. as_view() refuses a file spec declared many. The context carries presents_file where the spec, or any action, presents a file, and the shipped form renders hx-boost="false" for it, so the browser posts it natively.

The request is read through the same attributes and hooks as SpecView's, checked by the same code in http/utils.py: route_kwargs says which URL kwargs fill which parameters; get_pool_seeds(request), asked once per request, answers the seeds the class-level check, the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, the form's form_kwargs, the affordances and dispatch are handed; and get_server_arguments(request) answers the binding, laid over the route's arguments before the target is found and over the post's before dispatch. A field of the page's form the binding binds renders disabled with the server's value, and one it withholds disabled and empty, so the post never reads it. The seeds the spec's checks name are resolved once per request, by the kernel's resolve_seeds ahead of the class-level check, and its CallSeeds is handed to that check, the target's lookup and its checks, and dispatch, so each sees one value of each. The form's form_kwargs, the affordances' pool and a validated refresh's bind_arguments take no carrier, and resolve the seeds again: a resolver answering a fresh object answers each of those a different one.

The page's form is the Validator's, built with what its form_kwargs answers, through the kernel's form_keywords: on GET, on a refused post and for its own validation below, with the principal, the request's seeds, the row the post acts on and the request's one call context, the very dict dispatch is then handed. So a form whose __init__ takes a keyword - a queryset scoped by a tenant - is served, and the page's form offers the choices the Validator's accepts.

One call context per request: a plain dict the page creates for the request and hands, as the same object, to every kernel call it makes - the class-level check, the target's lookup and its checks, the affordances, the form's keywords and dispatch - so a check, a condition or the service declaring call_context reads what an earlier stage put there.

GET asks the spec's affordances once the target is found: the callable conditions always, through the kernel's unmet_operation_affordance on a pool built from the call's seeds, and, with none of those unmet and a row to ask about, the conditions on the row, as dispatch asks them. The first unmet Affordance is in the context as unavailable, for a template to read its code and reason; it is absent when every condition is met. On a page serving actions, each action's are asked, of the target the first action found, and unavailable is set only when no action is available (below). The post is dispatched as before, and dispatch's 409 stays the authority. A refused post's context carries code, the ActionUnavailable's, for a refusal carrying one, as error_response puts it in the JSON body; it is absent for every other. On a page serving actions it carries each action's state as GET does (below).

The page shows its target, on GET and on every refused post it re-renders, in the context beside the form: target is the row an instance selector found, or the set a collection_selector_spec resolved, and it is absent for a create and for a missing row allow_none lets through. A set comes with target_count, how many rows it held, and target_counted_at, when it was counted (django.utils.timezone.now()), so a template says "117 rows matched at 14:02" rather than promising a number the confirming post may not find. An empty set is no refusal: its scope check is asked, and the page counts 0. A queryset is counted by a COUNT on a fresh clone, never by reading its rows; the post re-runs the service on the set as it is then, and a refused one is counted again. A successful post counts nothing.

target_display is the target as a person reads it, on a page that sets display_target. It is off by default: an Output describes what the operation returns, which need not be its target, so a page presents its target only where it says the Output describes it. On, the target is presented through the spec's presenter - its own, or its output selector's - with the context dispatch hands it, projected by the kernel's project_payload, and with every HANDLE dropped as well as every HIDDEN one. A row's is a dict of its fields, with label, the value of the field marked LABEL, beside them where there is one, and pairs, the same fields as name and value in order, for a template to loop over, since fields.items reads a field named items; a set's is a list of those, one per row, for at most target_display_limit rows, read in one query. as_view() refuses a page displaying its target whose spec has no Output, whose Output marks none of its own fields with a FieldMarking, or whose markings the kernel's projection refuses, such as two labels. Whether the Output describes the target's rows is known only once one is presented: an Output that does not raises on the page's first request, which is the cost of turning the display on.

A refusal of the arguments shows every error in one post. Beside an InvalidArguments, the page's own form - built as the Validator's is, with the same keywords - is validated too, and the refusal is placed beside what it found, never twice. So after a shape-check refusal - a required field left blank, a date that does not parse - the form's further checks, a length, clean() or uniqueness, answer in the same post rather than the next. It is validated as the Validator validates its own, under the kernel's clean_held_to_their_columns, so a value no column holds - a key past 64 bits - is refused in the field's words and never reaches the database driver. With route_refusal_404 off, a post whose route the target's reads refuse never found its row, so its form is not judged as one and carries the refusal alone. Any other refusal is no verdict on the arguments - a conflict, a service's own rule, an unavailable action - and the page's form carries it alone, validated no further.

A partial spec's page renders no HTML required attribute, so the browser sends a post that leaves fields blank, and a blank field is absent: on a partial call, one the operation leaves as it is. A post with every field blank dispatches with no arguments but what a checkbox or a multi-select always sends, and is not refused. Beside a shape-check refusal, a partial page's form carries the refusal alone: its Validator takes the fields a post leaves out off its own form, and the page's form, validated whole, would call each one required.

One form, several operations. actions maps each submit button's name to the spec it runs, in place of spec. A committing post runs the action whose key request.POST carries, and one naming none or several is Django's BadRequest; GET, and a post that does not commit, render the first action's. success_url and success_message are page-wide, and get_success_url and get_success_message read the action that ran as self.action_name. The shipped template renders one button per action, named by its key. Every action is checked as spec is, and validated by a FormValidator of one form class.

Each action's button answers its own availability. GET asks every action's affordances, as above. The context carries unavailable_actions, each unavailable action's key mapped to its first unmet Affordance, absent when every action is available, and action_buttons, every action's key and that Affordance or None, in actions order, as pairs a template can loop over (an action keyed items would shadow a mapping's items). The shipped template disables an unavailable action's button and shows its reason beside its key, and the others stay usable. unavailable is the first action's Affordance only when no action is available, and then the form's fields are disabled too. A post naming an unavailable action is refused at 409 by its own dispatch, as on a page with one spec.

An action the user may not run is disabled, and says nothing. GET asks every action after the first the checks its post runs before dispatch: its admission and class-level permissions, then its object check on the row the page shows, or its scope check on a set or none, and, with route_refusal_404 on, a route capture its own parameters refuse. refused_actions is the frozenset of the keys refused, absent when none is; a refused action's affordances are not asked, so it is in neither unavailable_actions nor unavailable, and its action_buttons entry is None. The shipped template disables its button and gives no reason and no code. The first action's refusal is still the page's 403 or 404, and a post naming a refused action is refused as before. With the first action unavailable and every other refused, unavailable is not set: every button is disabled, and the form's fields are not.

A refused post's page keeps each action's state. A refused post's page carries unavailable_actions, refused_actions, action_buttons and unavailable as GET would, asked of the target that post found: the action that ran stands where GET's first does, and every other, the first included, is asked its checks and affordances as above, so a button GET disables stays disabled. With route_refusal_404 off, a post whose route the target's reads refuse found no target and carries none of them. A page with one spec carries no unavailable on a refused post.

A form over any Validator. form_class names the form a page renders for a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator. It is built as above, with get_form_kwargs() in place of form_kwargs, and read as above, and never validated: the Validator's refusal is the only error its form carries, so its clean(), field validators and uniqueness queries never run. success_message formats over the Validator's data, a mapping's keys or an object's attributes. as_view() refuses a form the post cannot be read off, a field or <name>-clear checkbox the spec does not declare, a required parameter neither the form, the server nor a tuple route_kwargs fills, a field whose type, element type, format where the spec names one, or required differs from its parameter's (any takes any field), a Validator with unsendable fields, form_class over a FormValidator, and a form defining its own clean() or clean_<field>(). Every action shares it.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a view with no ServiceSpec, a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator on a page with no form_class, a many spec, whose list of rows no form posts, a view with no success_url that does not override get_success_url, a commit_button that is not a button's name or is one of the form's fields, and a redirect_field_name that is not a key's name, is one of the form's fields or is the commit_button; and actions beside a spec, empty, keyed by anything but a non-empty string or by a field of the form, posting different form classes, keyed by the redirect_field_name, or beside any commit_button.

Sync only, in this release. CSRF is the host's middleware, as for any Django view, and the template renders {% csrf_token %}.

Bases: SpecPageBase

A ServiceSpec with no Validator, served as a page showing what it acts on and a button.

For an operation a person confirms rather than fills in - withdrawing a row, archiving a set - whose every argument the server answers: the route, a pool seed, a kwargs provider or server_arguments. The spec declares validator=None:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/withdraw/",
        SpecConfirmView.as_view(
            spec=withdraw_book_spec,
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            route_kwargs=("pk",),
        ),
    ),
]

What it shares with SpecFormView is everything but the form: the principal admitted by the class-level check before anything is shown, the target found as dispatch finds it - target, a set's target_count and target_counted_at, and target_display on a page that sets display_target - the affordances asked on GET as unavailable, commit_button, the fragment wrapper under htmx, the request hooks, success_url, redirect_field_name, success_message and a file's answer with as_attachment, each as SpecFormView documents it.

GET renders template_name with that context, beside view and spec, and no form: there is nothing to fill in, so the template renders its own <form method="post">, the CSRF token and the submit button. A key with nothing to hold is absent, as on every page, so {{ form }} is never None.

The page's template is optional, as on SpecFormView: django_spec_html/spec_confirm.html by default, which this package ships, with its button in django_spec_html/spec_confirm_fragment.html. It renders the target pane, an unmet affordance's reason with the button disabled, each action's own on a page serving actions, a refused post's errors or a question's message alone, and the button, posting commit_button's name where one is set, and the URL to return to as a hidden input where the view reads one. Found, refused at as_view() and overridden as SpecFormView's is.

POST dispatches with the route's kwargs, read by route_kwargs and coerced as a form page's are, under the binding and with the request's seeds. Nothing the post carries becomes an argument unless posted_arguments names it: not the CSRF token, not the button, not redirect_field_name's key and not any other key named like a parameter, so the closed argument set holds with nothing to check.

A bulk action reads its selection from the post. A list's button posting the ticked rows' checkboxes beside it, through hx-include, names their key in posted_arguments: ("ids",) for a spec taking ids. Each name is read from request.POST as a query string is read, every value of an array parameter and the last of anything else, a comma list split as the kernel's flat_arguments splits it and a blank absent, then merged with the route's and coerced by its declaration. A value refused, by coercion or by the shape check, is a refused post like any other: the page at 400, or under refusal_redirect its message and a redirect. Never a 404, which route_refusal_404 keeps for the route.

One page, several confirmations. actions maps each button's name to the spec it runs, in place of spec, as on SpecFormView: an "Archive" and a "Delete" button on one page, every action a spec with no Validator and checked as spec is. A post naming no action or several is a 400, GET renders the first action's spec, and the success hooks read self.action_name. Each action's button answers its own availability, in unavailable_actions and action_buttons as on SpecFormView: the shipped template disables an unavailable action's button and shows its reason, and the others stay usable; unavailable is set only when no action is. An action after the first the user may not run is disabled with no reason, its key in refused_actions, as on SpecFormView, and a refused post's page keeps each action's state, asked of the target that post found. as_view() refuses actions beside a commit_button: an actions page commits only through an action's button, and an action keyed like a posted_arguments name or csrfmiddlewaretoken, which a post carries whichever button it uses.

A success redirects to get_redirect_url() where the request names a safe URL to return to, else to get_success_url(result), or under htmx answers HX-Redirect to the same URL or the spec-result fragment, with success_message sent through django.contrib.messages where its middleware runs.

A refused post is the confirmation page again, at the status of the one map - 400 for an argument refusal, 409 for a conflict or an unavailable action, 422 for any other service refusal - or as the fragment at 200 under htmx, and needs no messages app. Its context carries errors, every message the refusal holds as a list of strings, a message about a parameter prefixed with its path ("pk: Enter a whole number."), and code for a refusal carrying one, and on a page serving actions each action's state as GET puts it. A denial is raised for the host's 403 or 404 page, as on any page.

A refused post may return where it came from instead. A button in a list's row posts to this page, and a refusal rendered here leaves the person on a page they never opened. With refusal_redirect, a refused post that is invalid, failed or a question sends each message of errors through messages.error, with the refusal's code as extra_tags where it has one, and redirects to get_refusal_url(refused): the safe URL redirect_field_name reads, else success_url. Under htmx it answers HX-Redirect to the same URL. A denial is raised as ever. Without the messages middleware there is nowhere to keep the messages, and a refusal with no message has nothing to send, so either is the page rendered as without refusal_redirect.

A question is shown, and cannot be answered here. A service raising AdditionalInputRequired re-renders the page at 422, its schema first checked by the kernel's check_requested_input, with requested_input - the message and the schema - and the message in errors. The page builds no control from a schema, and no post is read for an answer, so a confirming post is asked again. An operation that asks a person something mid-flight declares a form that holds the answer, and is served by SpecFormView with its asked_fields.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a spec with a Validator - a FormValidator's is SpecFormView's to serve - and a spec demanding a parameter that nothing but a post could supply, besides everything the page base refuses. Which parameters a call demands is the kernel's answer, through bind_arguments on a call carrying nothing, and each must be supplied by the route - a parameter route_kwargs names a kwarg into, since the URL pattern is not known when as_view() runs - by a seed the declared pool_seeds registers, as server_owned_keys reads them, or by a value server_arguments binds, or named in posted_arguments. A name there must be a parameter of the spec, and not one route_kwargs fills from the URL. It refuses refusal_redirect on a page with no success_url that does not override get_refusal_url, since a refused post naming no URL to return to would have nowhere to go.

docs.text:
Bases: SpecPageBase

A many ServiceSpec validated by a form, served as a formset, one form a row.

A many spec takes a list of rows under its many_argument, and the kernel validates the call per row: the shape check and the Validator run on each row, and a refusal is addressed by the row's index. So the page is a formset of the spec's form class: the Validator's formset_class where it declares one, so the rule over the whole set is declared once, else one formset_factory builds. The spec's Validator is a FormValidator, unless form_class names the row form:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/new/",
        SpecFormSetView.as_view(spec=add_books_spec, success_url=reverse_lazy("books")),
    ),
]

GET renders template_name with an unbound formset under formset, beside view and spec, once the spec's class-level check admits the principal, as SpecFormView's page does. The formset shows extra blank forms, after the spec's many_min_length forms, which a person must fill; and never more than many_max_length. The template renders {{ formset }} - its management form included - inside a POST form with its token.

The page's template is optional, as on SpecFormView: django_spec_html/spec_form_set.html by default, which this package ships, with its formset in django_spec_html/spec_form_set_fragment.html. It renders the management form, the formset's non-form errors, each form as a fieldset of its own with its errors, through django_spec_html/spec_form_set_row.html inside id="spec-form-set-rows", and the submit button posting commit_button's name where one is set, then the add_button, which skips the browser's checks since its post commits nothing, and carries hx-post, hx-target="#spec-form-set-rows" and hx-swap="beforeend", inert without htmx. No target pane. Found, refused at as_view() and overridden as SpecFormView's is.

No target pane. A many spec's rows are its forms, so display_target is refused at as_view() and the context carries no target_display. A spec with no collection_selector_spec has no set either, and no target or target_count.

An existing set is edited by a model formset. When the Validator's formset_class is a BaseModelFormSet, the page builds it with queryset= the collection target the spec's collection_selector_spec resolves on GET, one prefilled form a row, each posting its key, then the class's own extra blank forms; the management form's INITIAL_FORMS is the set's count. A post reads each initial form whole, its DELETE box with it, so a deleted row reaches the service with its key and DELETE true, and a row left out is left alone. as_view() refuses a model formset on a spec with no collection_selector_spec.

Every form is built as the Validator builds a row's, with what its form_kwargs answers, through the kernel's form_keywords: asked once per request, with the principal, the request's seeds and its one call context, and handed to every form as the formset's form_kwargs. There is no target to hand it, so the answer is the same for every row, and asking once is asking what each row would be asked. A form whose __init__ takes a keyword is served.

POST reads each form the formset bound, in the formset's order, as SpecFormView reads its one form - through its own widgets, a blank field absent, a disabled one not read - and sends the rows as one list under many_argument. The route's kwargs are read and coerced once for the call, beside the list, never inside a row. The management form's keys are the formset's, and never become arguments, as the CSRF token never does. An extra form left unchanged sends no row: the form Django would let through empty is not sent, so a page offering three blank forms posts only those a person filled in, and an extra form with its DELETE box ticked sends none, as Django's formset skips it. The first many_min_length forms are sent however they are left, so the kernel refuses a row left blank where the spec requires it. A post whose management form is missing or tampered with is refused before dispatch, in Django's own words, at 400.

A refusal is split back onto the forms. One addressed to row i of the list lands on the form that posted it, through add_argument_errors, so a dropped blank form shifts nothing; one about the list as a whole - its length, a message about the rows together - and one about a route value land on the formset's non_form_errors(), a route value prefixed with its name as on the single page. Beside an InvalidArguments each sent form is validated too, under the kernel's clean_held_to_their_columns, so every row's own checks answer in the same post; on a partial spec, and for any other refusal, the forms carry the refusal alone. Any other refusal's message is a non-form error, at the status SpecFormView answers it with.

A question is answered by its message alone. An AdditionalInputRequired is checked by the kernel's check_requested_input as on every page, so a schema no route could hear answered - a key declared only inside a row among them - raises ImproperlyConfigured and is never rendered. Then the formset is re-rendered at 422 with the message as a non-form error and requested_input, its message and schema, in the context, with no fields: a many call's top level is the list and the spec's reads, which no form declares, and the page builds no widget from a schema, so a once-for-the-call confirmation is not built on this page.

A post that does not commit, the fragment wrapper, the request hooks, the URL a success returns to under redirect_field_name and denials are SpecFormView's, by the same code: see that page. With commit_button set, add_button names a second submit button whose post is the page again with one more form, bound to everything posted, never past many_max_length, and nothing dispatched. An htmx add whose HX-Target is spec-form-set-rows, the shipped button's, is answered 200 with the new form alone - formset.empty_form at the next index, built with the same form_kwargs and rendered by the row template - then the management form's TOTAL_FORMS input with hx-swap-oob="true"; at many_max_length the answer is 204 with no body. Any other add, htmx included, is the formset again.

A formset over any Validator. form_class names the row form a page renders for a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator, as on SpecFormView: one formset_factory of it, bounded as above and built with get_form_kwargs() as every form's form_kwargs. Each form renders and is read as above, and is never validated: a row's refusal is the only error its form carries, and a refusal of the whole set, which the Validator's validated_many raises, lands on the non-form errors. The page adds no rule over the set of its own. On a spec with a collection_selector_spec the page edits the set it resolves, as a model formset does: one prefilled form a row, each posting the row's key under the model's primary key name, which the rows must declare, then the extra forms; INITIAL_FORMS is the set's count. Each initial form's row is sent with its key, a deleted one whole with DELETE true where the rows declare a boolean DELETE, which offers the box; a row left out is left alone, and a key missing or outside the set refuses its row on the form. as_view() checks the row form against the rows' parameters as SpecFormView checks its form against the spec's, except that a route or server_arguments fills the call's top level and never a row, so only the server's own keys fill a required row parameter the form leaves out.

A success message is success_message formatted with {"count": n}, the number of rows the call carried, so "%(count)d books were added." reads the post's own count. The single page formats with the cleaned data, and a many call's is a list, which % with a name cannot read. Override get_success_message to read result.data, the rows' cleaned data, or result.value.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator on a page with no form_class, a form_class the rows would not read, a spec that is not many, a view displaying its target, an extra that is not a non-negative int, an add_button that is not a button's name, that is set without a commit_button, or that is the commit_button; a redirect_field_name that is either button; and either button or the redirect_field_name named under the formset's form- prefix, which every post carries.

Sync only, in this release. CSRF is the host's middleware.

docs.title: SpecSelectorView
docs.text:
Bases: SpecRequestBase

A SelectorSpec served as a page: a list's rows a page at a time, or one row.

The read side of the pages: what a person browses, filters and picks a row from, declared once on the spec every other reader serves too. A LIST spec is a list page and a RETRIEVE spec the page of one row:

urlpatterns = [
    path("books/", SpecSelectorView.as_view(spec=books_spec)),
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/",
        SpecSelectorView.as_view(spec=book_spec, route_kwargs=("pk",)),
    ),
]

It is a spec's read page, not a model's list view: what it lists, who may see it, which filters it takes and what may be done to each row are the spec's, and the page adds only the paging and the wrapper.

GET, and HEAD, which Django answers by the same handler, are the methods it answers; anything else is 405. A request is:

  1. admitted, as every page admits it: the route checked against the spec's parameters, then the principal the class-level check admits, a denial raised for the host's 403 or 404 page. The seeds the spec's checks name are resolved there, once, by the kernel's resolve_seeds, and that check is asked on them;
  2. read by request_arguments' query-string branch - the URL kwargs under route_kwargs, the names server_arguments answers for dropped and then bound - as the JSON views read it, so a list page and a JSON list read each value the same way. A key the spec does not declare is ignored here, where the JSON views refuse it (see unknown_arguments). On a list, the paging keys are taken off first, so ?page=2 never reaches the spec;
  3. dispatched by the kernel's dispatch, with the grant the admission made, so the class-level check is asked once, and the seeds it resolved, so the checks dispatch asks and the selector see the values the class-level check saw;
  4. rendered with the raw rows dispatch answered, and no present(): a template reads the rows themselves.

The context. Beside view and spec:

  • rows: the rows served, a list. On a list page they are the page's rows, read in one query; on an instance page, the one row, or none for a RETRIEVE with allow_none that found nothing.
  • row: the one row, on an instance page that found one.
  • page: on a list page, the kernel's OutputPage - page, limit, total, total_pages, has_next - its items the same list as rows, so a template reading either reads no row twice. previous_page_query and next_page_query, where those pages exist, are the query the page read with the page key replaced, every filter kept, for a link's ?.
  • filter: the spec's filter_set, a django-filter FilterSet, bound to the query for display only, where the spec declares one.
  • table: table_class built over rows, where it is set.
  • row_displays: with display_rows on and no table_class, each row as its Output marks it for a person - label, fields and pairs, as the form page's target_display - with the raw row itself as row, so a template shows the one and asks available of the other.

Each row carries its affordances. Dispatch answers every row's affordances in bulk, as the spec's affordances declare them, and the page reads each row's answers once, so {% load django_spec_html %} and {% if row|available:"rename" %} asks a row what the operation's own dispatch would enforce, in no query of its own. See available.

Paging. A list is paged by the kernel's paginate_output: the page named by page_kwarg, paginate_by rows to a page, never more than max_page_size. A page that is not a whole number is page 1, and one past the last is the last, rather than a refusal: a public page clamps a link someone edited, and the page served says which it is. A client chooses the page size only where page_size_kwarg names the key it sends, bounded by max_page_size, which as_view() then requires; a value that is not a whole number is paginate_by, and a whole number below one is a page of one row, as paginate_output clamps it.

The query a page reads is get_query(request), the request's own query string unless a subclass answers another: a list that opens where the last visit left it reads a query the host kept in the session. The paging, the filter form, the spec's arguments and the links all read that one answer, and the template's request carries it as GET.

The filters are the spec's. filter.form is the FilterSet's form bound to the query for display, its own validation never run: dispatch reads the query, through the filter set's parameters, and is the one reader that decides, since two readers of one query string could disagree - django-filter's comma-separated filters split a value their own way.

A refusal is the page again, at the status of the one map: an argument refusal at 400, a precondition's ServiceError at 422, and so on, with errors, every message the refusal holds as a string, a message about a parameter prefixed with its path, and code for a refusal carrying one. The refusal is placed on filter.form too, an argument refusal at the fields it names. A denial is raised, for the host's 403 or 404 page, and a RETRIEVE that finds no row is Http404.

The fragment. An htmx request, unless boosted or a history restore, is answered with the results alone, at 200 whatever the outcome, as every page answers a fragment: fragment_template_name, or the spec-results fragment of template_name, or the shipped page's own fragment file. Every answer varies on the three headers that choice reads. A filter form's hx-get answered with it is a live search, and a next-page link's is a load-more.

A django-tables2 table is composed, never imported. table_class is built with the page's rows and order_by=(), so the table neither pages nor orders them: the spec ordered them, and paginate_output paged them. Its columns are not orderable unless table_order_by_field names the spec's own ordering parameter, which a header link then sets, for dispatch to read like any filter.

The page's template is optional: django_spec_html/spec_selector.html by default, which this package ships, its results in django_spec_html/spec_selector_fragment.html. It renders the filter form's fields, the table or each row's display, and the previous and next links. Found, refused at as_view() and overridden as SpecFormView's is.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a spec that is not a SelectorSpec and does not compile to one; the request hooks as every page refuses them; paging attributes of the wrong type, a client page size with no ceiling, and a list spec declaring a parameter under a paging key, whose value could never reach it; a table_order_by_field the spec does not declare, since no header link would then sort the rows; and display_rows on a spec whose Output cannot display a row.

The query string the page reads: request.GET unless overridden.

Asked once per request, and its answer is the one query the page reads: the paging keys taken off it, the filter form bound to it, the spec's arguments read from it, and the links built from it. The template is handed a request whose GET is this answer, so a tag building a link from request.GET, as django-tables2's header sort does, keeps it. A list that remembers its last filter, sort and page answers the session's copy on a bare visit, and saves a visit that sends anything:

class Remembered(SpecSelectorView):
    def get_query(self, request):
        if request.GET:
            request.session["books"] = request.GET.urlencode()
            return request.GET
        return QueryDict(request.session.get("books", ""))

A hook like this one saves the query before dispatch judges it, so a saved query the spec refuses - a filter value no longer valid - is refused on every bare visit until the host forgets it; the selector guide's example forgets it on ?reset=1.

A plain def, as as_view() requires of every request hook: the page does not await it. The answer must be a QueryDict, since the paging keys are popped off a copy of it as lists; anything else is a TypeError naming the hook. The answer is never changed in place (test_the_hook_s_answer_is_left_as_it_came).

available(row: Any, name: str) -> bool

Whether affordance name is available for row: {% if row|available:"rename" %}.

Read off what SpecSelectorView attached to each row it served - rows, row, each display's row and each record of its table - which is the kernel's row_affordance_answers, the flags dispatch answered for every row in bulk. So asking costs no query, and a row's button follows the rule the operation's dispatch enforces: the first of its conditions the row does not meet makes it unavailable.

A spec presenting no affordances declares none, so every name raises there. A row the page did not serve carries no answers and raises too, and so does one that cannot carry an attribute, such as a tuple from values_list().

The error is a TemplateSyntaxError, the template's own mistake, which Django reports with the template's line under DEBUG and no tag silences as a missing variable. But Django's {% if %} swallows it inside not, and, or or a comparison, reading the error as that whole expression being false, so {% if not row|available:"renmae" %} draws its branch for no row and raises nothing (test_a_misspelt_name_under_not_is_swallowed_by_django). docs.title: SpecActionsMixin
docs.text:
Bases: ModelAdmin

A ModelAdmin offering each spec in spec_actions as an action, on the spec's page.

Mixed in ahead of admin.ModelAdmin, or of any subclass of it, with one SpecAction per operation:

@admin.register(Book)
class BookAdmin(SpecActionsMixin, admin.ModelAdmin):
    spec_actions = (
        SpecAction("withdraw", withdraw_book_spec, "Withdraw", parameter="pk"),
        SpecAction("publish", publish_books_spec, "Publish", parameter="pks"),
    )

Which kind of action is the spec's target's answer. A spec with an instance_selector_spec is an object action: a link among the change page's object tools, to <object_id>/actions/<name>/, whose object_id fills the selector's parameter through the page's route_kwargs, unquoted as the admin quotes it. A spec with a collection_selector_spec is a changelist action: an entry in the action dropdown, which redirects to actions/<name>/ with the selected rows' primary keys in the query string, repeated under parameter. The page binds them to that parameter as server_arguments, read from the query string on GET and on the post the page sends back to its own URL, so nothing posted stands in for the selection; and the collection selector still decides the set, so a key it does not answer is not acted on.

The admin's scope comes first, as for its own actions and its change page: a page is served only to a principal holding the admin's view or change permission, the row's on an object action, and acts only on rows in the admin's get_queryset(). An object action's row outside it is a 404, and a changelist action's selection is narrowed to it before it is bound, so a key outside it never reaches the selector. Within that scope the spec's own checks run, and its selector decides the set.

Each page is the spec's own: SpecFormView for a spec validating with a FormValidator or an action whose page_kwargs carry a form_class, SpecConfirmView for one with none, built once when the admin is registered, so as_view() refuses then what it refuses of any page. Its URL is added by get_urls() ahead of the admin's own, wrapped in admin_site.admin_view(), so only a signed-in staff member the site admits reaches it; the page then admits the principal by the admin's permission and the spec's own checks, as on any route, and answers the rest with the host's 403 page. Its templates, django_spec_html/admin/spec_form.html and django_spec_html/admin/spec_confirm.html, extend admin/base_site.html with the admin's breadcrumbs and title around the very fragment the shipped page includes, so an htmx request is answered with that fragment, as on any page. A success returns to the row's change page or to the changelist, with the page's success_message among the admin's messages.

Offered only to a principal both admit. The object-tools link and the dropdown entry are shown only where the kernel's authorize, the spec's class-level check, admits the request's principal, asked with the page's own seeds and call context, and the admin's view or change permission does too. docs.title: SpecView
docs.text:
Bases: SpecViewBase

One spec as a view: each request it answers goes through dispatch_request.

Every attribute can be set on a subclass or passed to as_view():

urlpatterns = [
    path("notes/", SpecView.as_view(spec=list_notes_spec)),
    path("notes/<int:pk>/rename/", SpecView.as_view(spec=rename_note_spec)),
]

The methods follow the spec. A SelectorSpec answers GET and HEAD, a ServiceSpec POST, and methods replaces that with the ones it names, from GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. Any other method is Django's own 405, whose Allow header lists exactly the methods served, and OPTIONS is Django's own answer. The URL kwargs are arguments, merged last so the route wins a clash, which means the spec declares each one: a route capturing a kwarg its spec does not declare raises ImproperlyConfigured on the first request it serves, since that is the host's configuration rather than anything a client sent. route_kwargs renames or drops the kwargs a spec does not declare, as an include() prefix such as <org>/ needs.

The request reaches the call through two hooks, each defaulting to the attribute of its name: get_pool_seeds(request) for the seeds, so a tenant or a locale middleware resolved reaches a permission check, a selector or a Validator; and get_server_arguments(request) for the values the server answers for, which outrank whatever the client sent and whose names are the declared server_arguments' own. The view passes itself to dispatch_request as view=, so a spec callable naming request or view is handed this request and this view.

as_view() checks the configuration when the view is built, so a view with no spec, an async def hook, route_kwargs naming a parameter the spec does not declare or one the binding answers for, or a binding that cannot mean what it says, fails when the URLconf is imported rather than on its first request. Each request checks what only it can show: a captured kwarg the spec does not declare or the binding answers for, two kwargs filling one parameter, and the hooks' answers (see SpecViewBase.as_view).

CSRF is the host's middleware, as for any Django view. Nothing here is exempted, and csrf_exempt(SpecView.as_view(...)) is one line for a host that wants it.

Bases: SpecViewBase

SpecView, with every handler async.

The same attributes, methods, checks and answers, through adispatch_request. Django serves a class-based view async only when every handler it defines is async def, and refuses a class that mixes the two, so every method a spec may be served on is async here, not only the ones it answers by default. Under ASGI this keeps the request off a worker thread until the kernel needs one; under WSGI Django runs it in an event loop of its own, which costs more than SpecView and buys nothing.

get_pool_seeds and get_server_arguments stay sync methods, run in an executor hop of their own before dispatch, so an override reading request.user or a model is never a query on the event loop. as_view() refuses an async def one, which would never be awaited.

Not a subclass of SpecView, for the same reason: an async handler cannot stand in for a sync one.
