docs.title: dispatch_request
docs.text:
dispatch_request(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    request: HttpRequest,
    *,
    url_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    route_kwargs: Mapping[str, str | None] | tuple[str, ...] | None = None,
    server_arguments: ServerArguments | None = None,
    success_status: int | None = None,
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    view: Any = None,
) -> HttpResponseBase

Dispatch spec for request and answer it as JSON: the function a view calls.

  1. The principal is request.user, anonymous included, since the spec's permission check is what decides whether anonymous may act. An authenticated user whose is_active is false is refused as PrincipalUnavailable: a backend other than ModelBackend can log one in, and a deactivated principal never acts. Dispatch refuses one by the same rule; refusing here as well keeps the request unread for it.
  2. The arguments are request_arguments for spec.parameters(), with url_kwargs merged last under the names route_kwargs maps them to, and server_arguments applied over them by the kernel's apply_server_arguments: its bound values outrank whatever the client sent, and its withheld names are dropped. A URL kwarg filling one of its names is refused, as the host's misconfiguration. The binding is not checked here: a host's own view calls check_server_arguments once, when it is built, as SpecView.as_view() does.
  3. dispatch, with grant, pool_seeds and unknown_arguments as given, and a call context of its own holding request and view. So a spec callable naming request - a seed's resolver, a selector, a permission check, an affordance condition, a form_kwargs, the service - is handed this very request, and one naming view is handed view: the host's own view, which passes itself, as SpecView does, and None where it passes nothing (TestTheRequestAndTheView in test_dispatch_request).
  4. The answer. A not-found result is 404 with a detail. Otherwise the presented value, bare, at success_status if given, else 204 for a service with nothing to present and 200 for everything else - the defaults djangorestframework-services answers with. A 204 has no body.

A refusal of either family, from any of the four steps, is answered by error_response. Anything else propagates, a configuration error included: it is wrong for every caller, so it belongs to the host's error handling rather than to one client's response. A URL kwarg spec does not declare, and that route_kwargs neither renames nor drops, is one, raised as ImproperlyConfigured: every URL kwarg is an argument, and the route is the host's. So is a bound value its parameter refuses: the client neither sent it nor can see it.

spec may be a SpecSource: it is compiled once, first, and every step reads the spec it compiles to.

CSRF is the host's middleware, as for any Django view: nothing here exempts a view, and csrf_exempt is one line for a host that wants it.

docs.title: adispatch_request async
docs.text:
adispatch_request(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource,
    request: HttpRequest,
    *,
    url_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    route_kwargs: Mapping[str, str | None] | tuple[str, ...] | None = None,
    server_arguments: ServerArguments | None = None,
    success_status: int | None = None,
    grant: Grant | None = None,
    pool_seeds: PoolSeeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    view: Any = None,
) -> HttpResponseBase

dispatch_request, async.

The same principal, arguments, call context, statuses and refusals, and the same view, reached through adispatch and apresent, so the kernel's async rule holds: nothing that may query runs on the event loop.

That includes reading the request, which is one executor hop of its own before adispatch's. request.user is the lazy object AuthenticationMiddleware leaves, and its first read is a session query, which Django refuses on the loop; Django 4.2, the floor, has no request.auser() to await instead. spec.parameters() goes in the same hop, because a Validator may read a model to declare what it takes, and so does applying server_arguments, which reads it again.

A refusal asking for input is checked in a hop of its own for the same reason: the check holds the schema against spec.parameters(), read again for that call. Building the response does not query and stays on the loop.

docs.title: error_response
docs.text:
error_response(exc: DispatchError | ServiceError) -> JsonResponse

exc as JSON, at the status djangorestframework-services answers it with.

One map for both families, at djangorestframework-services' statuses, and the one the page reads too. Two bodies differ from its answer. A service's string or list detail, which DRF answers as a bare list and this as a field map under non_field_errors, so every 400 here has one shape. And an AdditionalInputRequired schema, which DRF reads as an error detail and so writes with every value a string ("minimum": "1"), and this writes as the JSON Schema it is:

  • InvalidArguments: 400, the error tree
  • ServiceValidationError: 400, its detail, as a field map
  • PermissionCheckDenied, NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable: 403, {"detail": message}
  • ServiceNotFound: 404, {"detail": message}
  • ActionUnavailable: 409, {"detail": message, "code": code}
  • any other ServiceConflict: 409, {"detail": message}
  • AdditionalInputRequired with a schema: 422, {"detail": message, "schema": schema}
  • any other ServiceError: 422, {"detail": message}
  • UnsupportedMediaType: 415, {"detail": message}
  • any other DispatchError: 400, {"detail": message}

Every 400 body is a field map. InvalidArguments is its tree, whose integer row keys JSON writes as strings. A ServiceValidationError's mapping is its body as it is, and a string or a list goes under non_field_errors, where a message about the input as a whole sits in the tree too. A lazy translation is one message, not a sequence of characters, and renders in the active language: JsonResponse's encoder renders every lazy string it meets, messages included.

Never 401. A session-authenticated view has no challenge to answer, and a 401 tells a client to start an authentication flow it has no way to finish. An anonymous caller a permission check refuses is a 403, like any other refused principal.

Two members add a key beside detail, and keep their base's status. ActionUnavailable is a conflict, and its arm exists only to put the affordance's code in the body beside the detail a client already reads: the stable code is the whole point of the member, and a client left with only the sentence has nothing to branch on. AdditionalInputRequired is "I need one more value", which is the operation being unprocessable as asked, so it stays a 422 like any other service error; the schema naming what is missing joins the body, because without it a client is told that something is needed and not what. Only when there is a schema: the error is valid without one, and growing the body unconditionally would change every plain message into an object for no gain.

A DispatchError no row names - raised by nobody in this package, or a subclass a later release adds - is still a refusal of the call rather than the operation's own verdict, so it answers 400 rather than 422.

docs.title: request_arguments
docs.text:
request_arguments(
    request: HttpRequest,
    parameters: Parameters,
    *,
    url_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    route_kwargs: Mapping[str, str | None] | tuple[str, ...] | None = None,
    server_arguments: ServerArguments | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]

The arguments a request carries for parameters, typed as a JSON caller would send them.

Where they are read from depends on the method and the body:

  • GET and HEAD: the query string, which is flat. Any body is ignored.
  • Any other method, with an application/json body: the body, read as it is. It must be a JSON object; an empty body is no arguments, as DRF's parser reads one. Its values are not coerced here: a "5" sent for an integer is the shape check's to read, as it reads one from any caller.
  • Any other method, with a form body (application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data): the fields, which are flat. Django parses one into request.POST for POST alone, so a PUT, PATCH or DELETE body is parsed here the same way rather than arriving empty. Any other body is refused as UnsupportedMediaType rather than read as none, since an operation whose parameters are all optional would then run with nothing; a request with no body carries no arguments, whatever its Content-Type says.

A flat source is read by the declaration, through the kernel's flat_arguments. A parameter of type array takes every value its key was sent with, and anything else takes the last, as QueryDict reads a repeated key. An array of numbers, integers, booleans or decimal strings also reads a value holding commas as its elements, ?ids=1,2 as [1, 2] with the space around a part trimmed, because a comma cannot be part of such a value and it is the spelling a django-filter CSV filter advertises; repeated keys and commas may mix. A decimal element stays the string it spells. An empty part (?ids=1,,2) is not dropped as a blank element is: it is refused at its index as any malformed element is. A string array is split only where its choices hold no comma, as an ordering's do, so ?o=title,-pk is ["title", "-pk"]; otherwise it is never split, since a comma is part of a string. An array is read no further than one element past the most it takes - its max_length, or the SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH setting's default - so a list over it is refused at its name as a whole, without a million commas becoming a million elements first; Django's DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_NUMBER_FIELDS counts keys, and a comma list is one. A blank value is absent unless "" is one the parameter can take: a plain string can, and a number, a boolean, a date, a decimal, or a string whose choices leave the blank out cannot. A flat wire has no other spelling of "left blank", and an empty ?count= or ?since= from a filter form is not a refusal to count or a malformed date. Each blank element of an array is read by the same rule, the whole array absent once nothing is left. Django's csrfmiddlewaretoken is dropped. What remains goes through coerce_flat, which leaves an undeclared key as it is, so the closed argument set in dispatch stays the one place that refuses it, under the caller's policy.

An upload is an argument, under the name its part carries, as each field is: the upload itself, Django's UploadedFile, for a parameter of type file, every upload under the name for an array, and the last of repeated ones for anything else. It replaces a field of the same name, since a browser sends a file input only as a file: a single value reads as the upload in DRF's merged data too, where an array there would hold the field and the uploads together. A POST's uploads are Django's own request.FILES; those in a PUT, PATCH or DELETE body are parsed here with its fields. An upload under a name parameters do not declare passes through like an undeclared field, for the closed argument set to refuse, and a file input left empty is no upload, so it is absent. Only a multipart body carries one.

URL kwargs are merged last, through coerce_flat as well since a path segment with no converter is a string. The route wins a clash, as it does in djangorestframework-services: a client-supplied value must not move the route's scope, so /notes/4/ with pk=9 in its body is about note 4. On a flat request the two are coerced together, so every refusal comes back at once and a clashing client value the route replaced is never refused. route_kwargs says which URL kwargs fill which parameters, renaming or dropping the rest, as route_arguments reads it.

Every name server_arguments answers for is dropped from what the client sent, before anything is coerced, so a client's ?owner=abc for a bound integer is never refused as the client's 400 for a name it was never offered. A URL kwarg filling one is refused instead, as the host's misconfiguration: the route is the host's, and it may not contradict the host's own binding, so a capture the spec should not read is dropped explicitly, with route_kwargs={name: None}. Only the names are read here: the values are laid by the kernel's apply_server_arguments, which needs the spec to check them, so a host's own view passes the result through it, as dispatch_request does.

Raises:

Type Description InvalidArguments

a JSON body that does not parse or is not an object, under non_field_errors; or coerce_flat's refusals, each at its parameter's name.

UnsupportedMediaType

a body that is neither JSON nor a form.

ImproperlyConfigured

a URL kwarg parameters does not declare, a route_kwargs naming a parameter they do not, or a URL kwarg filling a name server_arguments answers for, which is the host's route rather than the client's request; see route_arguments.

docs.title: route_arguments
docs.text:
route_arguments(
    parameters: Parameters,
    url_kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    *,
    route_kwargs: Mapping[str, str | None] | tuple[str, ...] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]

The kwargs a route captured, as arguments, each one a parameter the spec declares.

How request_arguments reads the route, public so that a host's own view reading the rest of its arguments some other way - a bound form, a page's own fields - merges the route by the same rule and refuses the same misconfiguration.

Every URL kwarg is an argument, so a route capturing one its spec does not declare is the host's configuration, wrong for every request the route serves, rather than anything a client sent. It is refused as one - Django answers it 500 and shows it under DEBUG - where a client's own undeclared argument is a 400. The unknown_arguments policy does not reach it: that policy is about what a client sends, and no client can send a route kwarg or stop sending one.

route_kwargs says which kwargs fill which parameters, for a route whose kwargs are not all the spec's, as an include() prefix such as <org>/ reaches every view under it:

  • None, the default, is the strict rule above, unchanged.
  • A mapping from a captured name to the parameter it fills, or to None to drop it: {"note": "pk", "org": None}. A captured name the mapping does not mention is still held to the strict rule, so a typo in the route is caught as before.
  • A tuple of names is an allow-list: each passes under its own name, and every other captured kwarg is dropped.

Every target a mapping names, and every name an allow-list lists, is a parameter the spec declares, checked whatever the route captured: the setting is the host's, the same on every route the view is mounted on. Two kwargs filling one parameter, a rename onto a name the route also captures, are refused as well, since neither could win honestly. A route kwarg is never a server value, whatever it fills: the client's URL chose it, so a malformed one is the client's 400, as anything a client sent is (test_a_renamed_kwarg_that_does_not_parse_is_the_clients_400).

Returned as a plain copy and uncoerced, so each caller merges it last, where the route wins a clash, and coerces it beside what the client sent: coerce_flat(parameters, {**read, **route_arguments(parameters, url_kwargs)}), so one refusal carries every problem with either.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

naming every undeclared kwarg, target or allowed name, in order; or a parameter more than one kwarg fills.

TypeError

route_kwargs is a bare string, which would otherwise be read as a tuple of its characters.

docs.title: request_principal
docs.text:
request_principal(request: HttpRequest) -> Any

request.user, anonymous included, unless it is a deactivated account.

How dispatch_request, adispatch_request and both spec views read the principal, public so that a host's own view - one rendering a page, or reading its arguments some other way - reads it by the same rule, and refuses before it reads anything else of the request.

Anonymous is passed through because a permission check is what decides whether anonymous may act, and the spec declares that check; refusing it here would make every spec's policy stricter than the one it states.

A deactivated account is refused, by the rule dispatch itself applies and resolve_principal applies off HTTP: ModelBackend never logs one in, but AllowAllUsersModelBackend and a project's own backend may. The rule asks about authenticated users alone, since AnonymousUser.is_active is False, and a custom user model with no is_active reads as active. Dispatch would refuse the same user; refusing here as well is what keeps the request unread for one, as adispatch resolves a principal_id before looking at its arguments.

Touching request.user evaluates the lazy object AuthenticationMiddleware leaves there, which is a session query, so an async caller calls this off the event loop, as adispatch_request does.

Raises:

Type Description PrincipalUnavailable

an authenticated user whose is_active is false.

docs.title: add_argument_errors
docs.text:
add_argument_errors(form: BaseForm, detail: Mapping[Any, Any]) -> None

Place a refusal tree on a bound form, beside the form's own errors, never twice.

detail is an InvalidArguments tree, or a ServiceValidationError's mapping. Each message goes where a person reading the form looks for it, through Django's public form.add_error:

  • A key naming one of the form's fields puts its messages on that field. A form is flat, so the only tree below a field is an array's element indices, which mean nothing to a person reading one control: the messages go on the field without them.
  • non_field_errors, and Django's own "__all__", go to the form's non-field errors as they are.
  • Any other key - a URL kwarg such as pk, or a key a service chose - goes to the non-field errors prefixed with its path, "pk: ...", so the reader knows what it is about. A nested tree is flattened to its leaves with the path joined by dots, "books.1.title: ...", a row's own non_field_errors adding nothing to the path.

Never a duplicate. A message the form already carries at the same place is not added again. The form validating the same data says the same thing the kernel does - a FormValidator's refusal is the form's errors, and the shape check spells its messages as Django's fields do - so without this most refusals would show twice. A form not yet validated is validated first, as reading form.errors would, so the form's own errors are always the ones compared against; but with the guards a FormValidator's form is validated with, since the form's own validation would hand the database driver a number no integer column holds, which SQLite's refuses with OverflowError. A model choice field's key past its column's range is refused as invalid_choice and a ModelForm's value past its integer column's range as max_value or min_value, in the words a FormValidator refuses them with, so the refusal of one is placed once (test_a_list_s_key_past_its_column_is_refused_once, test_a_model_form_s_integer_past_its_column_is_refused_once). A form already validated is compared as it stands.

A leaf is a message whatever its type: a string, a lazy translation (which is not a str, and is never taken apart into characters), or a list of either. The form must be bound, as Django's add_error requires.

A plain string, not a member of a kernel type: the kernel names no transport, and each package owns and exports its own value. docs.text:

A request carried a body that is neither JSON nor a form.

Refused rather than read as no arguments. Read as none, a PATCH sent as text/plain or application/merge-patch+json to an operation whose parameters are all optional would run with nothing and answer success, which tells its client the change was made. docs.title: Serving a read
docs.text:
A selector spec served as a page: a list of rows a person filters and pages through, or one row. SpecSelectorView admits the request as every page does, reads the query string as the spec's arguments, runs the kernel's dispatch, and renders the rows the selector returned. It answers GET and HEAD and nothing else, since a read changes nothing; an operation a row offers is a link to the page that runs it, such as a SpecConfirmView.

from django_spec_html import SpecSelectorView

The example lists books, filters them by title and author, and offers to withdraw a published one. Its specs:

@dataclasses.dataclass
class BookOut:
    """A book as a page names it."""

    pk: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]  # another call's input: never shown
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    status: Status


def book_by_pk(*, pk: int) -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.filter(pk=pk)


def withdraw(*, instance: Book) -> Book:
    instance.status = Status.DRAFT
    instance.save(update_fields=["status"])
    return instance


def withdrawals_open() -> bool:
    return not WITHDRAWALS_PAUSED


# The operation a row offers, with a condition of each kind: one on the row,
# answered for every row in the page's one query, and one over the seeds.
withdraw_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=withdraw,
    permissions=OPEN,
    instance_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE, selector=book_by_pk, reads=BY_PK
    ),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
    affordances=[
        Affordance(
            code="not_published",
            reason="Only a published book can be withdrawn.",
            when=Q(status=Status.PUBLISHED),
        ),
        Affordance(
            code="withdrawals_paused",
            reason="Withdrawals are paused.",
            when=withdrawals_open,
        ),
    ],
)


class BookFilters(django_filters.FilterSet):
    title = django_filters.CharFilter(lookup_expr="icontains")
    author = django_filters.ModelChoiceFilter(queryset=Author.objects.order_by("name"))
    o = django_filters.OrderingFilter(fields=("title", "price"))

    class Meta:
        model = Book
        fields: list[str] = []


def books() -> QuerySet[Book]:
    # The author joined in, since the table shows each row's author's name.
    return Book.objects.select_related("author")


book_list_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=books,
    permissions=OPEN,
    filter_set=BookFilters,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
    affordances={"withdraw": withdraw_book_spec},
)

book_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
    selector=book_by_pk,
    reads=BY_PK,
    permissions=OPEN,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
    affordances={"withdraw": withdraw_book_spec},
)

BookOut marks pk as the handle, another call's input that a page never shows, and title as the label, the name a page calls a row by.

and its URLconf, a list page, the same list as a table, a page for one book and the page that withdraws it:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/",
        SpecSelectorView.as_view(
            spec=book_list_spec,
            paginate_by=10,
            # A client may choose its page size, up to the ceiling.
            page_size_kwarg="per_page",
            max_page_size=50,
        ),
        name="books",
    ),
    path(
        "books/table/",
        SpecSelectorView.as_view(
            spec=book_list_spec,
            paginate_by=10,
            table_class=BookTable,
            # The filter set's OrderingFilter: each header link sends it.
            table_order_by_field="o",
        ),
        name="book-table",
    ),
    path("books/<int:pk>/", SpecSelectorView.as_view(spec=book_spec), name="book"),
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/withdraw/",
        SpecConfirmView.as_view(
            spec=withdraw_book_spec,
            success_url=reverse_lazy("book-table"),
            route_kwargs=("pk",),
            display_target=True,
        ),
        name="withdraw-book",
    ),
]

The module is a whole project's URLconf over the shipped templates, so it serves real pages: set ROOT_URLCONF = "docs.examples.spec_selector", list django_spec_html, django_tables2 and tests.adapter_app in INSTALLED_APPS, run manage.py migrate --run-syncdb (the test app ships no migrations), call docs.examples.spec_selector.seed() once from manage.py shell, and open /books/.

docs.title: What the page renders
docs.text:
as_view() refuses a spec that is not a SelectorSpec, or a source that does not compile to one, when the URLconf is imported, and points a write at the form pages. The context holds view and spec, as every page's does, and:

Key On a list On an instance page rows the page's rows the one row, or none where allow_none let a missing one through row - the one row page the kernel's OutputPage: page, limit, total, total_pages, has_next, and items, which is rows - previous_page_query, next_page_query the query string of each neighbouring page, where it exists - filter the spec's filter_set, bound to the query string the same row_displays each row with its label or pairs, as its Output marks it the same table the table_class table, where one is set the same errors, code on a refusal, in place of the rows the same

A key with nothing to hold is absent, so {% if page %} is false on an instance page. A row the selector does not find is Http404, as the form pages answer it.

The rows are the selector's own, never a presenter's copy: a template reads row.author.name off a Book it was handed. What a person is shown by default is each row as the spec's Output marks it - its label, or its fields with the handle left out - which is row_displays, presented with the context dispatch built for the call. So as_view() refuses a spec whose Output the page cannot display, unless the page is told it needs no display: table_class set, or display_rows = False for a template of the project's own.

docs.title: Paging
docs.text:
A list is paged by the kernel's paginate_output: one COUNT, then the page of rows, both clamped, so page 99 of three is page three and its links lead where their labels say.

Attribute Default page_kwarg "page" the query key naming the page paginate_by None, the kernel's 100 the page size max_page_size None the ceiling on any page size page_size_kwarg None a query key a client chooses the page size with, up to max_page_size, which it then needs

The paging keys never reach the spec. They are taken off the query before the spec reads it, so ?page=2 is the page's under either unknown_arguments policy, and as_view() refuses a list spec declaring a parameter under a paging key, since that parameter could never be sent. Rename the key with page_kwarg instead. A page that is not a whole number is page one, and a size that is not one is paginate_by. An instance page is not paged, so its query is all the spec's: there ?page=2 is an argument like any other.

The links keep every other key, the filters and a client's page size among them, and replace the page.

docs.title: A list that remembers its query
docs.text:
The query the page reads is get_query(request), which answers request.GET unless a subclass answers another QueryDict. The page asks it once a request and reads every key from its answer: the paging keys, the filter form, the spec's arguments and the links. A list that opens where the last visit left it keeps the query in the session:

class RememberedBooks(SpecSelectorView):
    """The book list, opened where this session's last visit left it."""

    def get_query(self, request: HttpRequest) -> QueryDict:
        # ?reset=1 forgets the saved query.
        if "reset" in request.GET:
            request.session.pop("books_query", None)
            return QueryDict()
        if request.GET:
            request.session["books_query"] = request.GET.urlencode()
            return request.GET
        return QueryDict(request.session.get("books_query", ""))


urlpatterns += [
    path(
        "books/remembered/",
        RememberedBooks.as_view(spec=book_list_spec, paginate_by=10),
        name="remembered-books",
    ),
]

A bare visit to /books/remembered/ serves the filters, the sort and the page of the visit before it, and its links keep them; a visit that sends any key is the query, and is saved in its place. The template is handed a request whose GET is the query the page read, so a tag building a link from request.GET keeps it too: a django-tables2 table's header sort links carry the remembered filters. The project needs Django's sessions installed, as the session is the host's and not the page's.

The hook saves the query before dispatch judges it. A saved query the spec refuses - a key it no longer declares under REJECT, or a filter value that is no longer valid, such as an author since deleted - is refused again on every bare visit. So the example forgets it on ?reset=1, which answers the list with no query at all; a page's "clear filters" link is that URL.

The hook is a plain def, as every request hook is, and as_view() refuses an async def one, since the page does not await it. An answer that is not a QueryDict raises TypeError naming the hook: the paging keys are popped off a copy of it as lists.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
A spec's filter_set is the page's filter form, as filter: bound to the query string for display, with the paging keys taken off. The page never validates it. Dispatch reads the same query through the same filter set and is the one reader that decides; its refusal is placed on that form by add_argument_errors, so filter.form.errors is the refusal, and an error the form would have raised in words of its own is not shown twice. A refused query renders the page at its refusal's status - 400 for a value the reads refuse - with the messages in errors and no rows.

The shipped page draws the form's fields with no errors beside them, and every message of a refusal in the results, so a page that swaps its results under htmx shows them too.

docs.title: A key the spec does not declare
docs.text:
Is ignored. SpecSelectorView.unknown_arguments is UnknownArguments.IGNORE, so ?utm_source=newsletter on a list page serves the rows as if it were not there, and beside a filter the filter is read as usual. The page links keep it, as they keep every key. The query string of a page a person reads is written by links the page does not control: a tracking parameter, a bookmark from before a filter was renamed. Refusing what the spec does not declare would answer that visitor a 400 for the link. It holds on an instance page too.

A key the spec does declare is still read by its declaration, so ?author=999 is refused at 400 whatever else the query carries, and a route kwarg the spec does not declare is the host's misconfiguration under either policy. The form and confirmation pages send dispatch only their form's fields and the route, so a query key they do not declare never reaches it; the JSON views refuse an undeclared key by default, since a client's code chose it rather than whoever wrote a link.

A list whose query is built by code alone opts back into the refusal:

# A list whose query only code builds, refusing a key the spec does not
# declare where the default would ignore it.
strict_book_list = SpecSelectorView.as_view(
    spec=book_list_spec, paginate_by=10, unknown_arguments=UnknownArguments.REJECT
)

which answers ?utm_source=newsletter with a 400 and utm_source: Unknown argument. on the page, placed on the filter form's non-field errors.

docs.title: What a row offers
docs.text:
A selector spec's affordances name the operations a row offers, and dispatch answers every condition for every row in the page's one query: a Q as an annotation on it, a callable once. The page attaches those answers to each row it serves, and the available filter reads them:

{% load django_spec_html %}
{% for row in rows %}
  {{ row.title }}
  {% if row|available:"withdraw" %}<a href="{% url "withdraw-book" row.pk %}">Withdraw</a>
  {% else %}<span>Not available</span>{% endif %}
{% endfor %}

So the button follows the rule the operation's own dispatch enforces, and asking costs no query. A name the spec does not declare raises TemplateSyntaxError, naming those it does, rather than reading as unavailable for good.

Read a negated or combined condition through {% with %}. Django's {% if %} reads an error raised inside not, and, or or a comparison as the whole condition false, so {% if not row|available:"withdarw" %} draws nothing and raises nothing. {% with %} resolves the filter outside {% if %}, so the same misspelt name raises there:

{% with ok=row|available:"withdraw" %}
  {% if not ok %}<span>Not available</span>{% endif %}
{% endwith %}

A filter on its own, {% if row|available:"withdraw" %}, raises as it is. The same holds for unavailable, below.

A row that is a mapping, such as one from values(), is answered on a copy, so a selector's own rows are left as they were. A row that cannot carry an attribute, such as a tuple from values_list(), is served without answers, and either filter raises for it.

A row that wraps its model instance, a frozen dataclass for one, is answered as well when the spec declares row_object, which the kernel reads once for every transport: the answers are put on the wrapper past its frozen guard, so row|available:"withdraw" and row|unavailable:"withdraw" read it unchanged, and the answers come from the same one query dispatch already made for every row. A wrapper with __slots__ has no place to carry them and is served without answers, as a tuple is.

docs.title: Why a row's action is unavailable
docs.text:
The unavailable filter reads the same answers and says why: the row's answer, with the code and reason of the first condition the row does not meet, when the action is unavailable, and None when it is available. It costs no query either, and raises for the same names and rows.

{% with why=row|unavailable:"withdraw" %}
  {% if why %}<span title="{{ why.code }}">{{ why.reason }}</span>
  {% else %}<a href="{% url "withdraw-book" row.pk %}">Withdraw</a>{% endif %}
{% endwith %}

A condition on the row asked of a row that no longer exists answers with no code and no reason, since none of the conditions' sentences is true of it: why is still the answer, so {% if why %} holds, and {{ why.reason }} renders as any missing variable does. The answer is a dict, so {{ why|json_script:"why" }} hands it to a script, and a fresh copy per read whose clear and popitem no template can call, so a template cannot empty it.

A row's action refused or gone is the host's to answer, for htmx too, by the handlers in a denial under htmx.

docs.title: A django-tables2 table
docs.text:
table_class names a django-tables2 Table. The page builds it over the rows it served, as table, and the shipped template includes the table's own template. The package does not depend on django-tables2: install it and list django_tables2 in INSTALLED_APPS in a project that sets table_class.

class BookTable(tables.Table):
    title = tables.Column()
    # Not among the OrderingFilter's fields, so its header links no sort.
    author = tables.Column(accessor="author__name", verbose_name="Author", orderable=False)
    price = tables.Column()
    # The button where the row may be withdrawn, and otherwise why not.
    withdraw = tables.TemplateColumn(
        '{% load django_spec_html %}{% with why=record|unavailable:"withdraw" %}'
        "{% if why %}<span>{{ why.reason }}</span>"
        '{% else %}<a href="{% url "withdraw-book" record.pk %}">Withdraw</a>{% endif %}'
        "{% endwith %}",
        orderable=False,
        verbose_name="",
    )

A TemplateColumn asks each record what it offers, as a template asks a row: the example's shows the button, or the reason it is not there. The table never pages or orders the rows: they are the spec's page, in the spec's order. It is built with no request, since django-tables2 then runs its RequestConfig, which would page and order the data from the query string, and with order_by=(), so a Meta.order_by is never applied.

With no table_order_by_field, no column is orderable and no header links a sort. Set it to a parameter the spec declares - a filter set's OrderingFilter, o in the example - and each orderable column's header links ?o=<column>, which dispatch reads as any other argument. as_view() refuses a field the spec does not declare. A table whose Meta sets a prefix links the prefixed key, ?t-o=<column> for a prefix of t-, so that key is the one the spec must declare. Mark a column the filter cannot order by orderable=False, as the example's author is: its link would send a value the OrderingFilter refuses, and answer 400.

Two limits follow from the table never being told the order. A header always links the ascending sort, so a second click does not reverse it; a link reversing it is the template's to write, from filter.form. And a header link keeps the page the person was on, where a new order usually starts again from page one.

The shipped page includes the table's template rather than calling {% render_table %}, which the package does not load, so a TemplateColumn renders without the page's context, and a {% csrf_token %} in one renders nothing. A form posting from a column belongs on a template of the project's own that renders the table with {% render_table table %}.

docs.title: A file
docs.text:
A RETRIEVE spec whose presenter is the kernel's FilePresenter is a download rather than a page: the row it finds is presented through the presenter, and the answer is the file, a FileResponse of its bytes or file object, or a StreamingHttpResponse for an iterable of bytes, with the presenter's content type and Content-Length wherever the size is known.

invoice_pdf = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
    selector=invoice_by_pk,
    reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)),
    presenter=FilePresenter(
        "application/pdf",
        filename=lambda invoice: f"invoice-{invoice.pk}.pdf",
        render=render_invoice_pdf,
    ),
)

path(
    "invoices/<int:pk>/pdf/",
    SpecSelectorView.as_view(spec=invoice_pdf, route_kwargs=("pk",)),
)

Content-Disposition is attachment, naming the file, quoted by RFC 5987 for a name outside ASCII; as_attachment = False answers inline, so a browser shows a PDF in place. An htmx request is answered the file too. The admission, the route and every refusal are the page's as for any other read; an allow_none spec that finds nothing renders the page with no row, and no display is asked of a spec whose Output is a file.

as_view() refuses a file presented by a LIST spec, through the kernel's file_output: a list of files has no answer on any transport.

docs.title: An htmx request
docs.text:
An htmx request is answered with the results alone, spec_selector_fragment.html by default or the template's spec-results partial, as the form pages answer with their form (an htmx request). A refusal is the fragment at 200, since htmx swaps no 4xx by default, and every response carries Vary: HX-Request. The shipped page wraps its results in <div id="spec-results"> and adds no hx- attribute of its own; a live search is the project's:

<form method="get" hx-get="" hx-target="#spec-results" hx-trigger="input changed delay:300ms">
  {{ filter.form }}
</form>

docs.title: How many queries a page costs
docs.text: A list page costs the same number of queries whatever its size: the COUNT, the page of rows with every row's affordance flags annotated on it, and whatever the template asks of its own - in the example, the author filter's choices. The example's tests hold three queries for both its pages at three books and at thirty. A query per row is the template's, from a relation the selector does not join, which is why the example's books() selects the author the table shows.

docs.title: Server arguments, seeds and route values
docs.text: As on every page: a route's captured values are arguments, pool_seeds and get_pool_seeds add to the call's seeds, and server_arguments fills a parameter from the server's side, outranking a value the query string sends (the request). The seeds the spec's checks name are resolved once for the request, before the class-level check, and dispatch runs on them, so that check, the check dispatch asks of the rows and the selector see one value of each.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: What this package says to a person reads in the language active where it is said: the pages' own text (Save, Confirm, Search, Previous, Next, the page counts), and the words of the refusals it raises or answers, such as UnsupportedMediaType's default message and The request body is not valid JSON.. Each is a msgid, looked up in the active language when it is shown, so nothing is fixed at import. A message the caller passes, UnsupportedMediaType("Send JSON."), is shown as given.

docs.title: The source catalog
docs.text:
The package ships its source catalog, django_spec_html/locale/en/LC_MESSAGES/django.po: every msgid it marks, the Python gettext calls and the templates' {% translate %} and {% blocktranslate %} text alike, untranslated. It is the file a contributed language starts from, and it is generated (make messages), never edited by hand. No translated language ships.

Django loads a catalog only from an app in INSTALLED_APPS or from a directory in LOCALE_PATHS. The pages' templates are found only when django_spec_html is listed in INSTALLED_APPS (installing), so a project using them has this package's catalog loading already, and a language compiled beside the source catalog is used with nothing more. A project that gives every page a template_name of its own, or uses only the JSON views, and does not list the app loads none of it; list the app, or add a catalog to LOCALE_PATHS.

docs.title: The kernel's refusals
docs.text:
The refusals this package maps onto a response are the kernel's (NotPermitted, InvalidArguments, ServiceNotFound and the rest), and their messages are the kernel's catalog. It loads only when django_service_specs is listed too:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # ...
    "django_service_specs",
    "django_spec_html",
]

The translations section of the kernel's home page says which of its msgids are DRF's own, so that a project with DRF installed keeps DRF's translation of them.

docs.title: Keeping one catalog
docs.text:
A project that keeps every translation in its own catalog, under LOCALE_PATHS, cannot have makemessages collect these msgids: it reads the project's source and never site-packages, and it marks each msgid it did not find there obsolete. So combine the template it writes with each package's source catalog, and merge that into each language, after every makemessages run and every upgrade of this package:

HTML_PO="$(python -c 'import importlib.util, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(importlib.util.find_spec("django_spec_html").origin).parent / "locale/en/LC_MESSAGES/django.po")')"
django-admin makemessages --locale de --keep-pot
msgcat --use-first locale/django.pot "$HTML_PO" --output-file locale/django.pot
msgmerge --update --backup=none locale/de/LC_MESSAGES/django.po locale/django.pot
django-admin compilemessages --locale de

msgmerge brings back each translation the makemessages run had marked obsolete, so a msgid translated once stays translated. --use-first keeps the project's own header and, for a msgid both catalogs hold, the project's entry. Add the kernel's source catalog to the msgcat line the same way to carry its msgids into the one catalog.
